title: Contents

paper.title: Contents
paper.abstract: Abstract Sampling high-dimensional probability distributions is a central task in scientific computing, with applications ranging from Bayesian inference to statistical physics and molecular simulation. Despite decades of methodological developments, two major challenges remain: scaling to high dimensions and efficiently exploring multimodal distributions characterized by metastable states. Classical approaches such as Markov chain Monte Carlo, tempering methods, or enhanced sampling based on collective variables have achieved major successes, but they also face intrinsic limitations. This tutorial review explores a new paradigm that has recently emerged at the interface of machine learning and computational statistical physics: the use of generative models as tools for sampling. In this context, models such as normalizing flows and diffusion models are not used in their traditional data-driven setting, but rather as flexible probabilistic models that can assist the sampling of distributions known only up to a normalization constant. This manuscript reviews the early development of this rapidly evolving field and discusses several methodological directions, including exact samplers based on generative models and strategies to train such models in the absence of data. While an exhaustive survey of the literature is not attempted, we present a selection of key ideas and methods, along with a discussion of their strengths and limitations. The review is intended to be an accessible tutorial for both physics and machine learning audiences, and it aims to provide a starting point for researchers interested in exploring this exciting area of research.

sections.heading: Sampling and its challenges
sections.text: Sampling is a fundamental task in scientific computing, as it enables the efficient approximation of high-dimensional integrals. In observational and experimental sciences, for instance, sampling is essential for uncertainty quantification and model calibration through Bayesian inference. In theoretical physics, sampling is an indispensable computational tool for studying many-body systems across a broad spectrum of applications, ranging from lattice gauge theory for the strong nuclear force to quantum Monte Carlo methods for solving the Schrödinger equation or investigating the thermodynamic properties of materials. The task of sampling consists in generating realizations of a random variable according to a given target distribution. In this tutorial, we focus on the common setting where the state space is continuous and the probability density function—denoted by π \pi throughout—is known up to a normalization constant. Sampling from π \pi shares certain features with optimization: both require identifying the most probable regions of the state space, typically located near local maxima of the target density. Crucially, however, sampling must also correctly capture fluctuations around these maxima and reproduce the relative weights of different regions. It is therefore a fundamentally different problem from optimization, with its own intrinsic challenges. The first modern sampling algorithms emerged in the early 1950s, enabled by the advent of digital computers. The Metropolis algorithm [ 115 , 175 , 114 ] was the first Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method and laid the foundation for a vast family of techniques that followed. Since then, an extensive literature has developed, proposing a wide variety of algorithms tailored to the diverse challenges arising across application domains and target distributions (see, e.g., [ 107 ] for a comprehensive introduction). To this day, two major sources of difficulty remain central: scalability , the ability to handle high-dimensional target measures, and metastability —also referred to as multimodality—the presence of multiple well-separated local maxima in the measure. MCMC methods can often cope with moderately high-dimensional spaces by exploring the state space through random walks. However, their essentially local exploration mechanism typically makes transitions between distant high-probability regions highly unlikely. As a result, the chain may remain trapped for extremely long times in so-called metastable states. A striking illustration is provided by protein folding: although the folded configuration corresponds to the global minimum of the Boltzmann free energy, locating this free-energy minimum by sampling the associated Boltzmann distribution with traditional, local molecular dynamics or MCMC methods is essentially impossible in practice, as the dynamics remains trapped in long-lived metastable intermediates.

sections.heading: Important families of sampling algorithms to tackle metastability in high dimension
sections.text: To clarify why metastability is such a difficult problem, it is useful to briefly review the main families of sampling algorithms that have been developed to address it. Non-local jump samplers. As previously mentioned, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods typically rely on local proposals. While this ensures reasonable scalability with dimension, it severely limits mixing in the presence of metastability, making transitions between modes exponentially rare with respect to the energy barriers separating them. To address this issue, various approaches have been proposed to incorporate non-local moves. In certain specific settings, remarkably effective solutions have been developed. In lattice spin systems with discrete variables, cluster algorithms such as the Swendsen-Wang [ 164 ] and Wolff [ 180 ] updates enable collective moves of large groups of spins and can dramatically accelerate sampling close to the critical region despite of a diverging correlation length. In the context of particle systems, several non-local strategies have also proven highly effective. Swap Monte Carlo [ 72 , 18 ] —which proposes exchanges of particle identities in addition to local displacements—can accelerate equilibration of glass-forming systems by many orders of magnitude. Event-chain Monte Carlo [ 16 ] , a rejection-free irreversible algorithm that propagates displacements through chains of particles, has likewise led to major improvements in the simulation of dense particle systems. Meanwhile, the statistics literature has attempted to construct general-purpose mode-hopping proposals [ 169 , 139 ] . However, designing effective non-local proposals in general is challenging as it requires identifying high-density regions that typically occupy an increasingly small fraction of the state space as the dimension grows. Simple parameterizations of such proposals, such as Gaussians or mixtures of Gaussians, usually fail in high dimension, since these approximations remain too crude and lie too far from the true target distribution. Annealing-based samplers. A more robust family of methods for sampling complex distributions is based on tempering, also known as annealing. The central idea is to define a sequence of intermediate distributions that bridge a simple base distribution and the complex target distribution. This bridge is commonly constructed by gradually increasing an effective temperature or weakening interactions between variables until reaching an independent (product) measure. The resulting path is then exploited to progressively transport samples toward the target, which can substantially improve exploration in multimodal settings. Among the most widely used tempering-based methods are annealed importance sampling (AIS) [ 125 ] , parallel tempering (PT, also known as replica exchange) [ 163 , 64 , 85 ] , and sequential Monte Carlo (SMC, also known as population annealing) [ 84 , 46 ] . Despite their effectiveness, annealing-based methods present practical challenges. Notably, the choice of a suitable annealing path and of the number of intermediate distributions have a decisive impact on performance. Self-adaptive SMC [ 34 ] provides a principled mechanism to adjust the number of steps dynamically and is among the most effective algorithms currently available for multimodal targets. However, annealing-based methods may still struggle when the reference measure differs too drastically from the target distribution. In protein conformational sampling, for example, high-temperature annealing may lead to complete denaturation, so that configurations obtained at high temperature carry little useful information about the folded state. Similarly, in statistical mechanics, the presence of a discontinuous (first-order) phase transition along the annealing path can break the connection between high- and low-temperature regimes, rendering the bridge ineffective. Thus, while annealing-based samplers represent the state of the art for addressing multimodality, alternative strategies remain necessary — in particular in situations where constructing a suitable annealing path is difficult, or where one may hope to bypass annealing altogether through more direct and potentially more efficient approaches. Dimensionality reduction to enhance sampling. Another classical strategy to tackle high-dimensional multimodal sampling problems consists in identifying a low-dimensional projection of the full configuration space — often referred to as a set of collective variables (CVs), or equivalently a coarse-graining of the system — that resolves the different modes of the target distribution. Sampling across these modes is then driven by forcing the exploration in the CV space which is typically of much lower dimension than the full space. These approaches, particularly popular in molecular simulation, come in many variants; a recent review can be found in [ 77 ] . However, these techniques face two major challenges. First, they are mostly restricted to very low-dimensional CV spaces, since the non-parametric estimation of the marginal distribution they rely on becomes rapidly intractable as the dimension of the reduced space increases. Second, identifying an appropriate set of collective variables — that is, a suitable low-dimensional projection capable of separating the relevant metastable states — is itself a difficult task, especially under stringent dimensionality constraints. Going beyond these different families of samplers for multimodal distributions, and building on recent advances in machine learning, a new paradigm for sampling has begun to emerge, leveraging the expressive power of generative models to learn complex probability distributions and produce representative samples. In the following, we aim to present the main ideas and results in this rapidly developing field. In what sense do these methods overcome the limitations discussed above? How can they be combined with classical approaches? What challenges and open questions remain?

sections.heading: Generative modelling vs sampling
sections.text: Let us first clarify the difference between generative modelling and sampling, as these two terms are often used interchangeably in the literature. Generative modelling consists in learning a probabilistic model -- namely the generative model -- given an extensive set of samples from an unknown distribution. It is a fundamentally data-driven task of density estimation, where the goal is to learn a model that can generate new samples that are similar to the training data, this similarity being not necessarily well-defined 1 1 1 For one thing, the distribution most faithful to a training dataset is the sum of Dirac deltas at the training points. . In contrast, sampling is the task of generating samples from a target distribution whose probability density function is known (possibly up to a normalizing constant). The task is different in two fundamental ways: (i) instead of a large dataset, information must be extracted from the knowledge of the mathematical expression of the target measure and little if any data is available; (ii) the objective is to produce samples that are exactly distributed according to the target measure, which has a well-defined mathematical meaning.

sections.heading: Generative models for scientific computing
sections.text: Generative models per se are highly flexible probabilistic models, usually parametrized via deep neural networks, which were primarily developed for generative modelling tasks on images and text, with the incredible successes we know. They have also already proven successful in data-driven computational tasks in physics and chemistry, such as protein folding with AlphaFold [ 92 ] and predicting protein-ligand binding structures [ 39 ] . Here, we will discuss how generative models are also proving to be powerful tools for sampling. Pioneering works in this direction [ 105 , 5 , 132 ] have demonstrated that subclasses of generative models, namely normalizing flows and autoregressive networks, can rather easily be repurposed for exact sampling by enabling reweighing of the generated realizations with respect to the target measure. Proofs of concept have been shown for various areas of physics and chemistry, including lattice quantum field-theories [ 1 ] , biomolecules [ 132 ] or, in sampling nano-clusters of heavy atoms at quantum accuracy [ 119 ] . These early successes have also uncovered important limitations of such direct reweighing strategies, and have spurred the development of more sophisticated approaches. As a result, a broad landscape of methods has emerged, ranging from refined flow-based constructions to the most recent diffusion models adapted to sampling tasks. This diversity has created a rapidly evolving “zoo” of techniques in which conceptual connections are not always transparent and methodological differences can be subtle. In this tutorial review, we survey a representative subset of these approaches with the aim of clarifying their underlying principles, highlighting their common structure, and emphasizing the trade-offs they entail. While striving to remain concise, we focus on the core ideas and main results, and refer the reader to the original works for technical details and further developments.

sections.heading: Previous partial reviews of sampling with generative models
sections.text: As the field continues to gain momentum, any attempt at exhaustiveness would be futile. Nevertheless, assembling the first chapters of this rapidly developing story can be valuable, particularly for newcomers seeking an entry point into the subject. Also, several works have already attempted to summarize specific aspects of the field. Chapter 7.2 of the textbook [ 42 ] , coordinated by Anna Dawid following a doctoral school on machine learning for quantum physics held in September 2021, reviews early developments in the use of generative models for many-body physics. The lecture notes by Eric Vanden-Eijnden for the Les Houches Summer School on Statistical Physics & Machine Learning (August 2022) introduce foundational principles of sampling with generative models [ 8 ] . The commentary [ 37 ] discusses the pioneering work [ 132 ] on Boltzmann generators and its immediate extensions. More focused reviews include [ 40 ] , which surveys advances with specific applications to lattice quantum chromodynamics, [ 76 ] , which places different diffusion-based sampling approaches into perspective and [ 145 , 134 ] , which reviews the use of generative models for molecular dynamics simulations.

sections.heading: 1.3 Outline of the review
sections.text: The “pipeline” of sampling with generative models can be decomposed into three main stages, which will guide the structure of what follows. The first stage (i) consists in choosing a suitable family of generative models, typically a transport-based model, such as a normalizing flow or a diffusion model, or an autoregressive model. Section 2 briefly reviews these generative models, both for completeness and to introduce the notations used throughout the manuscript. It also recalls how these models are traditionally trained from data in the standard “generative modelling” setting. The next two stages in sampling with generative models are (ii) training the generative model in the specific context of sampling, where no data is available, and (iii) designing sampling algorithms that leverage the trained model to generate samples from the target distribution. These two stages are closely intertwined. In particular, as we will see, the training procedure can itself exploit the sampling capabilities of the generative model. For this reason, the exposition does not strictly follow the chronological order of the pipeline, but instead adopts an organization that we believe makes the underlying ideas clearer. Section 3 focuses on the design of exact sampling algorithms, assuming that a generative model has already been trained. This section concentrates in particular on algorithms based on exact-likelihood generative models, “discrete-time” normalizing flows and autoregressive models, which were the first generative models to be used for sampling and provide a transparent setting to understand the core principles. We move from early, straightforward reweighing strategies to more sophisticated approaches aimed at extending the scope of these methods, notably in the presence of metastability. Section 4 then takes a step back to examine the training of generative models for sampling. Starting with procedures originally developed for “discrete-time” normalizing flows, we discuss how these ideas extend to more recent classes of models, such as continuous normalizing flows and diffusion models. Section 5 returns to the design of sampling algorithms, this time focusing on recent developments involving “continuous-time” normalizing flows and diffusion models. Section 6 concludes with perspectives on the field and points to directions of interest that were not covered in this review.

sections.heading: 2 A brief introduction to generative models used for sampling
sections.text: We start with a brief review of the different types of generative models used to assist Monte Carlo sampling, introducing the notations employed throughout the rest of the review. These models are of two kinds: autoregressive models, which generate samples sequentially, and transport-based models, which transform samples from a simple base distribution into complex outputs. These generative approaches are particularly well-suited for sampling tasks as they give more or less direct access to the probability density of the generated samples, which is a key ingredient to build exact samplers from generative models as we will discuss in Section 3 . In this section, we focus on the traditional setting of generative modelling, where a dataset of training samples is available while their underlying target distribution is unknown. In Section 4 , we will discuss how to train generative models in the absence of data, which is the relevant setting for sampling tasks where instead the target distribution is known up to a normalization constant.

sections.heading: 2.1 Autoregressive models
sections.text: Autoregressive models (ARMs) are generative models that factorize the joint distribution of a random vector X = ( X 1 , … , X d ) ∈ 𝒳 X=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d})\in\mathcal{X} into a product of univariate conditional distributions. The probability density function, or the probability distribution if 𝒳 \mathcal{X} is discrete, is parameterized as ρ θ ​ ( x ) = ∏ i = 1 d ρ θ , i ​ ( x i ∣ x < i ) , \displaystyle\rho_{\theta}(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{d}\rho_{\theta,i}(x_{i}\mid x_{<i}), (1) where x < i = ( x 1 , … , x i − 1 ) x_{<i}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1}) denotes the vector of the first i − 1 i-1 components of x x , and ρ θ , i \rho_{\theta,i} is a learnable conditional distribution with parameter vector θ ∈ Θ \theta\in\Theta . Any joint distribution, for any ordering of the coordinates, can be factorized in this autoregressive fashion. However, the finite expressiveness of the parametric families of ρ θ , i \rho_{\theta,i} , built in practice with neural networks, renders the model sensitive to the choice of ordering which can be treated as an hyperparameter. Examples of choices of parametrizations for the conditional distributions ρ θ , i \rho_{\theta,i} are given by [ 63 , 171 ] . Within this autoregressive framework, sampling is performed sequentially, by first sampling x 1 ∼ ρ θ , 1 x_{1}\sim\rho_{\theta,1} , then x 2 ∼ ρ θ , 2 ( ⋅ ∣ x 1 ) x_{2}\sim\rho_{\theta,2}(\cdot\mid x_{1}) , and so on until x d ∼ ρ θ , d ( ⋅ ∣ x < d ) x_{d}\sim\rho_{\theta,d}(\cdot\mid x_{<d}) . Moreover, owing to their tractable probability (density), autoregressivee models can be trained for density estimation via maximum likelihood. Given a dataset of training samples { x ( k ) } k = 1 N \{x^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{N} assumed to be i.i.d. from an unknown target probability distribution π \pi , one learns parameters θ \theta of the NF by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the training set, θ ∈ arg ⁡ min − ∑ k = 1 N log ⁡ ρ θ ​ ( x ( k ) ) . \displaystyle\theta\in\arg\min-\sum_{k=1}^{N}\log\rho_{\theta}(x^{(k)}). (2) This approach has been successfully applied in various domains, including image generation and natural language processing. However, autoregressive models are mainly used for discrete state spaces, as for continuous state spaces they tend to be less flexible than transport-based models, which we discuss in the next sections.

sections.heading: 2.2.1 Original formulation
sections.text: Normalizing flows (NFs) were introduced by Tabak & Vanden Eijnden [ 165 ] as a method for density estimation on ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , based on learning the transport map from an empirical distribution toward a simple, typically Gaussian, base distribution, hence the name normalizing flow. More generally, denote ρ 0 \rho_{0} the density of the base distribution on the state space 𝒳 ⊂ ℝ d \mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} , and T θ T_{\theta} a diffeomorphism on 𝒳 \mathcal{X} with parameter vector θ ∈ Θ \theta\in\Theta . A NF is a learnable probabilistic model with realizations x x sampled through, z ∼ ρ 0 , x = T θ ​ ( z ) , \displaystyle z\sim\rho_{0},\quad x=T_{\theta}(z), (3) and associated probability density function given by the change-of-variables formula, ρ θ ​ ( x ) = ρ 0 ​ ( T θ − 1 ​ ( x ) ) ​ | det ∇ ( T θ − 1 ​ ( x ) ) | . \displaystyle\rho_{\theta}(x)=\rho_{0}\left(T_{\theta}^{-1}(x)\right)\left|\det\nabla\left(T_{\theta}^{-1}(x)\right)\right|. (4) According to Brenier’s theorem [ 22 ] , provided that ρ 0 \rho_{0} is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure, there exists, for any absolutely continuous target distribution π \pi , a transport map T ∗ T^{*} that pushes forward ρ 0 \rho_{0} to π \pi . This theoretical result justifies the use of transport maps as generative models, as they are, in principle, capable of representing arbitrary target distributions. In practice, however, the expressivness of the model depends on the chosen parametrization for T θ T_{\theta} . The central challenge is therefore to design parametrized maps T θ T_{\theta} that are sufficiently expressive while allowing efficient evaluation of the inverse map and the determinant of its Jacobian. To this end, normalizing flows are typically constructed as compositions of simpler transformations T θ = T θ L ∘ … ∘ T θ 1 , \displaystyle T_{\theta}=T_{\theta_{L}}\circ\ldots\circ T_{\theta_{1}}, (5) each T θ i T_{\theta_{i}} interpreted as a layer involving learnable neural networks and L L being the number of layers, or depth, of the NF. The so-called coupling layer trick is behind many popular architectures for these simple invertible transformations, with prominent examples including real non-volume preserving flows (RealNVP) [ 49 ] and neural spline flows (NSF) [ 52 ] . Comprehensive reviews of design choices for NFs can be found in [ 135 , 101 ] . For training in the traditional generative modeling setting, the negative log-likelihood of a training dataset { x ( k ) } k = 1 N \{x^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{N} can be minimized: θ ∈ arg ⁡ min − ∑ k = 1 N log ⁡ ρ θ ​ ( x ( k ) ) , \displaystyle\theta\in\arg\min-\sum_{k=1}^{N}\log\rho_{\theta}(x^{(k)}), (6) which is available in closed form thanks to the change-of-variables formula ( eq. 4 ) and architectures designed to allow efficient evaluation of the inverse map and the determinant of its Jacobian. While extremely convenient for density estimation, these architectures can nevertheless prove too restrictive when the target distribution is highly complex and multimodal. To overcome this issue, the more recent continuous normalizing flows rely on continuous-time dynamics to define the transport map. By opposition, the original NF architecture are sometimes referred to as discrete-time normalizing flows.

sections.heading: 2.3 Diffusion models
sections.text: CNFs trained by maximum likelihood encourage the velocity field to match the model final time marginal ρ θ , T \rho_{\theta,T} to the data target distribution, without imposing constraints on the intermediate ρ θ , t \rho_{\theta,t} distributions. In contrast, diffusion models (DMs) prescribe a noising-denoising path for the intermediate distributions to follow. For simplicity, we consider here the case 𝒳 = ℝ d \mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^{d} and an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) noising process defined by the stochastic differential equation (SDE) d ​ X ~ τ = − X ~ τ ​ d ​ τ + 2 ​ d ​ W ~ τ , X ~ 0 ∼ π , \displaystyle\mathrm{d}\tilde{X}_{\tau}=-\tilde{X}_{\tau}\mathrm{d}\tau+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{W}_{\tau},\quad\tilde{X}_{0}\sim\pi, (12) where W ~ τ \tilde{W}_{\tau} is a standard Brownian motion and π \pi denotes the unknown target distribution from which the training set is sampled. In what follows, the marginal distribution of the noising process at time τ \tau is denoted π τ \pi_{\tau} . The forward OU process — equivalently, an overdamped Langevin equation with quadratic confining potential — admits the Gaussian 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 d , I d ) \mathcal{N}(0_{d},I_{d}) as unique invariant measure and converges to it at an exponential rate. Consequently, one can assume that π T ≈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 d , I d ) \pi_{T}\approx\mathcal{N}(0_{d},I_{d}) for T ≫ 1 T\gg 1 . Anderson [ 10 ] established that the process defined in backward time t = T − τ t=T-\tau by d X t = ( X t + 2 ∇ log π T − t ( X t ) ) d t + 2 d W t , X 0 ∼ π T ≈ 𝒩 ( 0 d , I d ) , \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t}=\big(X_{t}+2\nabla\log\pi_{T-t}(X_{t})\big)\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}W_{t},\quad X_{0}\sim\pi_{T}\approx\mathcal{N}(0_{d},I_{d}), (13) admits π T − t \pi_{T-t} as its marginal density at time t t , which can be readily verified using the Fokker-Planck equation. In other words, the process defined in eq. 13 has the same marginal distributions as the noising process but evolves backward in time, and is therefore referred to as the denoising process. As originally proposed by [ 160 ] , a generative model can be constructed by running the backward denoising process starting from samples drawn from the limiting distribution of the noising process — here the standard Gaussian ρ 0 = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 d , I d ) \rho_{0}=\mathcal{N}(0_{d},I_{d}) — playing the role of the base distribution by analogy with normalizing flows. However, the denoising process defined in eq. 13 involves the gradient of the logarithm of the time-marginal density, known as the score . Let’s examine the score closely. The conditional distribution of the noising process at time τ \tau given the initial state x 0 x_{0} , denoted p τ | 0 ( ⋅ ∣ x 0 ) p_{\tau\mid 0}(\cdot\mid x_{0}) , is Gaussian, yielding the time marginal π τ ​ ( x ) \displaystyle\pi_{\tau}(x) = ∫ d ​ x 0 ​ p τ | 0 ​ ( x | x 0 ) ​ π ​ ( x 0 ) = ∫ d ​ x 0 ​ 𝒩 ​ ( x , x 0 ​ e − τ , ( 1 − e − 2 ​ τ ) ​ I d ) ​ π ​ ( x 0 ) , \displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}x_{0}\;p_{\tau|0}(x|x_{0})\,\pi(x_{0})=\int\mathrm{d}x_{0}\;\mathcal{N}(x;\,x_{0}e^{-\tau},\,(1-e^{-2\tau})I_{d})\,\pi(x_{0}), (14) where 𝒩 ⁡ ( ⋅ , m , Σ ) \mathcal{N}(\,\cdot\,;m,\Sigma) denotes the density of a Gaussian distribution with mean m m and covariance Σ \Sigma . From here, the score can be written as a conditional expectation over the initial state, using Bayes formula to recognize the conditional measure: ∇ log ⁡ π τ ​ ( x ) \displaystyle\nabla\log\pi_{\tau}(x) = − 1 π τ ​ ( x ) ∫ d x 0 x − x 0 ​ e − τ 1 − e − 2 ​ τ 𝒩 ( x ; x 0 e − τ ; ( 1 − e − 2 ​ τ ) I d ) π ( x 0 ) \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\pi_{\tau}(x)}\int\mathrm{d}x_{0}\;\frac{x-x_{0}e^{-\tau}}{1-e^{-2\tau}}\,\mathcal{N}(x;\,x_{0}e^{-\tau};\,(1-e^{-2\tau})I_{d})\,\pi(x_{0}) = − ∫ d x 0 x − x 0 ​ e − τ 1 − e − 2 ​ τ p τ | 0 ​ ( x ∣ x 0 ) ​ π ​ ( x 0 ) π τ ​ ( x ) \displaystyle=-\int\mathrm{d}x_{0}\;\frac{x-x_{0}e^{-\tau}}{1-e^{-2\tau}}\,\frac{p_{\tau\mid 0}(x\mid x_{0})\pi(x_{0})}{\pi_{\tau}(x)} = − 𝔼 x 0 [ x − x 0 ​ e − τ 1 − e − 2 ​ τ | X ~ τ = x ] . \displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{x_{0}}\left[\left.\frac{x-x_{0}e^{-\tau}}{1-e^{-2\tau}}\right|\tilde{X}_{\tau}=x\right]. (15) As a result, the score is doubly intractable: in generative modeling tasks, the target distribution π \pi is unknown and only accessible through an empirical training dataset. Additionally, even in sampling applications when π \pi is known, the conditional expectation remains a high-dimensional integral without a closed-form expression. In generative modeling applications, however, the score can be regressed directly from training data, typically using a neural network parametrization s θ : 𝒳 × [ 0 , T ] → 𝒳 s_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\times[0,T]\to\mathcal{X} . Its expression as a conditional expectation ( 15 ) motivates the denoising score matching objective introduced in [ 162 , 79 ] , which takes the form of a mean-squared error at a fixed time τ \tau , min θ ⁡ 𝔼 x 0 ​ [ ​ 𝔼 x | x 0 ​ [ ​ ‖ ​ s θ ​ ( x , τ ) + x − x 0 ​ e − τ 1 − e − 2 ​ τ ‖ 2 ] ] , \displaystyle\min_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{x_{0}}\left[\rule{0.0pt}{22.0pt}\mathbb{E}_{x\mid x_{0}}\left[\rule{0.0pt}{20.00003pt}\left\|\rule{0.0pt}{15.00002pt}s_{\theta}(x,\tau)+\frac{x-x_{0}e^{-\tau}}{1-e^{-2\tau}}\right\|^{2}\;\right]\right]\,, (16) where the reversed order of the expectations compared to 15 stems from the law of total expectation and reflects the practical implementation of the loss. An empirical approximation of this loss is constructed using samples x 0 x_{0} from the training set and samples of the form X ~ τ = x 0 ​ e − τ + 1 − e − 2 ​ τ ​ ξ \tilde{X}_{\tau}=x_{0}e^{-\tau}+\sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}}\,\xi with ξ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 d , I d ) \xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0_{d},I_{d}) drawn from the conditional distribution of the noising process p τ | 0 ( ⋅ ∣ x 0 ) p_{\tau\mid 0}(\cdot\mid x_{0}) . A weighted integral of this loss over τ ∈ [ 0 , T ] \tau\in[0,T] is commonly employed in practice, enabling the simultaneous training of the score across all time marginals. Presented here with the canonical illustration of the OU process, this noising-denoising construction admits many natural generalizations. Different forward diffusions can be considered, for instance the variance-exploding SDE, which relies on a purely diffusive process without drift, in contrast to the variance-preserving OU dynamics. We refer in particular to [ 95 ] , which clarifies several important design choices underlying the practical success of diffusion models, including noise scheduling, discretization schemes and neural architectures used to parametrize the score. Beyond modifications of the forward diffusion, alternative noising processes can also be employed. In particular, Schrödinger bridges — which achieve convergence in finite time and relax the assumption of a Gaussian base distribution — can be leveraged within the same noising-denoising paradigm for generative modelling [ 43 ] . Motivated by this idea of finite-time constructions and increased flexibility, another class of models — stochastic interpolants or flow matchings — has recently attracted attention in the generative modelling community. They offer a flexible framework that interpolates between prescribed endpoint distributions and will be the focus of the next section.

sections.heading: 2.4 Stochastic interpolants a.k.a. flow matchings
sections.text: The idea of constraining the path of intermediate distributions, has inspired the development of another class of transport-based continuous-time generative models, proposed independently in [ 7 , 108 , 106 ] . Here, we adopt the most general formulation of stochastic interpolants (SIs) introduced in [ 6 ] . While the base distribution of diffusion models is necessarily given by the limiting distribution of a noising process, the base distribution of stochastic interpolants (SIs), denoted ρ 0 \rho_{0} in the following, can be any distribution that is easy to sample from. The bridge of distributions is no longer defined through an SDE, but, instead, constructed using an interpolation function I t : [ 0 , 1 ] × 𝒳 × 𝒳 → 𝒳 I_{t}:[0,1]\times\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X} together with a positive scalar function γ : [ 0 , 1 ] → ℝ + \gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^{+} , X t = I t ​ ( X 0 , X 1 ) + γ ⁡ ( t ) ​ Z , X 0 ∼ ρ 0 , X 1 ∼ π , Z ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 d , I d ) . \displaystyle X_{t}=I_{t}(X_{0},X_{1})+\gamma(t)Z,\quad X_{0}\sim\rho_{0},\quad X_{1}\sim\pi,\quad Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0_{d},I_{d}). (17) The interpolation function satisfies I 0 ​ ( x 0 , x 1 ) = x 0 I_{0}(x_{0},x_{1})=x_{0} and I 1 ​ ( x 0 , x 1 ) = x 1 I_{1}(x_{0},x_{1})=x_{1} , the noise amplitude vanishes at the extremities, γ ⁡ ( 0 ) = γ ⁡ ( 1 ) = 0 \gamma(0)=\gamma(1)=0 , and suitable regularity conditions are required on both functions (see [ 6 ] , Definition 2.1). With this construction, the marginal distribution of X t X_{t} at time t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] is given by ρ t ​ ( x ) = ∫ d ​ x 0 ​ d ​ x 1 ​ 𝑑 z ​ ρ 0 ​ ( x 0 ) ​ π ​ ( x 1 ) ​ 𝒩 ​ ( z , 0 , I d ) ​ δ ​ ( x − I t ​ ( x 0 , x 1 ) − γ ⁡ ( t ) ​ z ) , \displaystyle\rho_{t}(x)=\int\mathrm{d}x_{0}\,\mathrm{d}x_{1}\,\mathrm{d}z\,\rho_{0}(x_{0})\,\pi(x_{1})\,\mathcal{N}(z;0,I_{d})\,\delta\left(x-I_{t}(x_{0},x_{1})-\gamma(t)z\right), (18) where π \pi is the target data distribution and δ \delta denotes the Dirac distribution. Although this marginal density is generally intractable, sampling from the interpolation process is straightforward, as it only requires sampling from the base distribution, the target data distribution (of which the training data are samples), and the Gaussian noise. To construct a generative model, one observes that the velocity field defined as the conditional expectation v ∗ ( x , t ) = 𝔼 x 0 , x 1 , z [ ∂ t I t ( x 0 , x 1 ) + γ ˙ z | X t = x ] , \displaystyle v^{*}(x,t)=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1},z}\left[\left.\partial_{t}I_{t}(x_{0},x_{1})+\dot{\gamma}z\,\right|\,X_{t}=x\right], (19) where γ ˙ \dot{\gamma} denotes the time derivative of γ \gamma , satisfies the continuity equation associated with the interpolating path of distributions eq. 18 : ∂ ρ t ​ ( x ) ∂ t + ∇ ⋅ ( ρ t ​ ( x ) ​ v ∗ ​ ( x , t ) ) = 0 . \displaystyle\frac{\partial\rho_{t}(x)}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot\Big(\rho_{t}(x)v^{*}(x,t)\Big)=0\,. (20) As a consequence, the deterministic process ( X t ∗ ) t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] (X_{t}^{*})_{t\in[0,1]} defined by the ODE d ​ X t ∗ d ​ t = v ∗ ​ ( X t ∗ , t ) , X 0 ∗ ∼ ρ 0 , \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}X_{t}^{*}}{\mathrm{d}t}=v^{*}(X^{*}_{t},t),\quad X^{*}_{0}\sim\rho_{0}, (21) admits the same time marginal distributions ρ t \rho_{t} as the interpolation process at all times. This observation enables the construction of a generative model by learning a neural network approximation v θ : 𝒳 × [ 0 , 1 ] → 𝒳 v_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\times[0,1]\to\mathcal{X} of v ∗ v^{*} . As for the score of diffusion models, the conditional expectation form of the target velocity field leads to a mean-squared regression loss at a fixed time t t , min θ 𝔼 x 0 , x 1 , z [ ‖ v θ ( X t , t ) − ( ∂ t I t ( x 0 , x 1 ) + γ ˙ z ) ‖ 2 | X t = I t ( x 0 , x 1 ) + γ ( t ) z ] . \displaystyle\min_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1},z}\left[\left.\left\|v_{\theta}(X_{t},t)-\big(\partial_{t}I_{t}(x_{0},x_{1})+\dot{\gamma}z\big)\right\|^{2}\right|X_{t}=I_{t}(x_{0},x_{1})+\gamma(t)z\right]. (22) In practice, an empirical approximation of this loss is obtained by drawing samples x 1 x_{1} from the training set, samples x 0 x_{0} from the base distribution, Gaussian noise samples z z , and averaging the mean squared error over (uniform or weighted) samples of time t t in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Once the velocity field has been learned, new samples are generated by integrating the ODE driven by v θ v_{\theta} from samples of the base distribution ρ 0 \rho_{0} up to time t = 1 t=1 . This sampling procedure boils down to the sampling procedure of CNFs, with the key difference that the velocity field is explicitly trained to match a prescribed interpolation path of distributions. Avoiding the maximum likelihood training of CNFs, this approach is significantly more efficient computationally. The generation process can also be generalized to a stochastic differential equation, at the cost of additionally regressing the score of the time marginals (see [ 7 ] , Corollary 2.9). A commonly used choice for the interpolation process is the noiseless linear interpolation I t ​ ( x 0 , x 1 ) = ( 1 − t ) ​ x 0 + t ​ x 1 I_{t}(x_{0},x_{1})=(1-t)x_{0}+tx_{1} , as proposed in [ 108 , 106 ] who introduced the denomination of flow matching for this particular case. Intermediate summary With this, we reviewed the main generative models that will be used in the sampling methods described in the rest of the text. Autoregressive models and normalizing flows both offer direct access to the likelihood of generated samples and can be trained by maximum likelihood. Yet, they are limited in expressivity and difficult to make compatible with symmetries. Continuous-time generative models, on the other hand, are more expressive and can be made compatible with symmetries, but computing their likelihood is challenging. Relying on the notations and mathematical tools introduced in this section, we now turn to the application of these different models to sampling problems.

sections.heading: 3 Exact samplers with exact likelihood generative models
sections.text: Normalizing flows (NF) and autoregressive models (ARM) were the first generative models to be repurposed from generative modelling to the task of sampling. As we will see below, their tractable likelihood allows to use them as helpers in a variety of Monte Carlo scheme in the place of traditional simple probabilistic models such as Gaussians or factorized distributions. In all described approaches, the first step is to train a generative model to approximate the target distribution of interest π \pi on the state space 𝒳 \mathcal{X} . While this training is not trivial given the absence of direct samples from the target a priori, we postpone the discussion on training strategies to the next section. In this section, we assume access to an ARM or a NF defining a distribution or probability density ρ θ \rho_{\theta} (respectively given by eq. 1 and eq. 4 ) which, loosely speaking, is close to π \pi . It is cheap to evaluate the likelihood ρ θ \rho_{\theta} of these models and to sample from them. We also assume that π ⁡ ( x ) \pi(x) is easy to compute up to a normalization constant, for any x ∈ 𝒳 x\in\mathcal{X} . Note that even if the agreement between ρ θ \rho_{\theta} and π \pi is imperfect — as is inevitably the case in practice due to approximation and optimization errors — the samplers described below remain exact. In other words, they generate samples from π \pi in the limit of large sample sizes or many iterations. This makes the present application of deep learning to scientific computing rather distinctive: the unavoidable imperfections introduced during the learning stage do not necessarily translate into biased results, provided that the subsequent sampling procedure is properly designed. Below, we first describe a set of simple approaches originally proposed to leverage ARMs and NFs for sampling ( section 3.1 ), and then discuss the advantages and limitations of these approaches in a systematic benchmark ( section 3.2 ). We then review more recent approaches looking to push further the abilities of samplers powered with exact likelihood models ( sections 3.3 and 3.4 ). Part of our discussion will only apply to NFs only as the samplers exploit their transport construction.

sections.heading: Elementary algorithm
sections.text: A simple way to leverage ARMs and NFs for sampling is to use them as proposal distributions in importance sampling (IS). For a target distribution π \pi , known up to a normalization constant, the IS estimation of the expectation of an observable f : 𝒳 → ℝ f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} follows the steps: algorithm 1 Neural importance sampler (Neural-IS) for i = 1 ​ … ​ N i=1\ldots N do Sample the proposal distribution x i ∼ ρ θ ​ ( ⋅ ) x_{i}\sim\rho_{\theta}(\cdot) , Compute weight w i = π ⁡ ( x i ) ρ θ ​ ( x i ) w_{i}=\frac{\pi(x_{i})}{\rho_{\theta}(x_{i})}\, (up to a multiplicative constant), for i = 1 ​ … ​ N i=1\ldots N do Compute normalized weight w ^ i = w i / ∑ j = 1 N w j \hat{w}_{i}=w_{i}/\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j} , return self-normalized IS estimator f ^ SNIS = ∑ i = 1 N w ^ i ​ f ​ ( x i ) \hat{f}_{\text{SNIS}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat{w}_{i}f(x_{i}) A practical IS proposal needs (i) to be straightforward to sample from to obtain an extensive set of N N i.i.d. samples easily and (ii) to have a tractable probability density function to compute weights, both conditions being satisfied by NFs. Note that if the normalization constant of π \pi is unknown, the IS weights can only be computed up to a multiplicative constant which however cancels in the self-normalized weights and hence has no impact on the self-normalized IS estimator f ^ SNIS \hat{f}_{\text{SNIS}} returned by the algorithm. Conversely, were the normalization constant of π \pi known, one could use the plain IS estimator f ^ IS = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N w i ​ f ​ ( x i ) \hat{f}_{\text{IS}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}f(x_{i}) which is unbiased, unlike the self-normalized version. Under mild conditions on the proposal distribution, f ^ SNIS \hat{f}_{\text{SNIS}} is a consistent estimator of 𝔼 π ​ [ f ] \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[f] in the sense that it converges (at least in probability) to 𝔼 π ​ [ f ] \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[f] as N → ∞ N\to\infty . However, at finite N N , the agreement of the proposal distribution ρ θ \rho_{\theta} with the target π \pi directly impacts the quality of the IS estimator. In particular, the variance of the IS weights is minimized when ρ θ \rho_{\theta} is equal to π \pi , yielding normalized weights uniformly equal to 1 / N 1/N . This observation justifies the relevance of leveraging recent progress in deep generative models, in the form of ARMs and NFs, to build accurate proposals in place of usual simple tractable probabilistic models (e.g. Gaussian or factorized). In turn, the quality of the IS estimator is directly related to the quality of the generative model’s approximation of the target distribution. Pioneering works in this direction include [ 122 , 132 , 129 , 127 ] .

sections.heading: Free energy computations
sections.text: Building on similar ideas of IS, one can also use exact likelihood models to estimate normalization constants, or free energies in the language of statistical mechanics. The idea is to use the generative model as a reference state of known normalization constant and estimate its ratio with normalization constant of the target π \pi using either Target Free Energy Perturbation (TFEP) [ 89 ] or Bennett Acceptance Ratio (BAR) [ 15 , 74 ] . This idea was simultaneously proposed with Bayesian inference in mind [ 90 ] , and for applications to atomic solids [ 177 , 179 , 178 , 152 ] . Computations of protein-lingand binding free energies with NFs were also explored in [ 49 ] , as well as computations of conformal free energy differences in [ 119 , 133 ] . By convention, the normalization constant of a NF or an ARM is 1 due to writing ρ θ \rho_{\theta} directly in its normalized form. For π ⁡ ( x ) = e − U ⁡ ( x ) / 𝒵 π \pi(x)=e^{-U(x)}/\mathcal{Z}_{\pi} , the TFEP estimator of its free energy F π = − log ⁡ 𝒵 π F_{\pi}=-\log\mathcal{Z}_{\pi} is build upon the equality 𝒵 π = 𝔼 ρ θ ​ [ e − U ⁡ ( x ) / ρ θ ​ ( x ) ] ⇒ F π = − log ⁡ 𝔼 ρ θ ​ [ e − U ⁡ ( x ) / ρ θ ​ ( x ) ] \displaystyle\mathcal{Z}_{\pi}=\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{\theta}}\left[e^{-U(x)}/\rho_{\theta}(x)\right]\quad\Rightarrow F_{\pi}=-\log\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{\theta}}\left[e^{-U(x)}/\rho_{\theta}(x)\right] (23) and reads F ^ π TFEP = − log 𝒵 ^ π TFEP = − log ( 1 N ∑ i = 1 N e − U ⁡ ( x i ) ρ θ ​ ( x i ) ) , with x i ∼ ρ θ ( ⋅ ) for i = 1 , … , N , \displaystyle\hat{F}_{\pi}^{\text{TFEP}}=-\log\hat{\mathcal{Z}}_{\pi}^{\text{TFEP}}=-\log\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{e^{-U(x_{i})}}{\rho_{\theta}(x_{i})}\right),\quad\text{with }x_{i}\sim\rho_{\theta}(\cdot)\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,N\;, (24) where one recognizes the IS weights w i w_{i} in the summation. This estimator is easy to implement, requiring mere samples from the flow and yields an unbiased estimator 𝒵 ^ π TFEP \hat{\mathcal{Z}}_{\pi}^{\text{TFEP}} of 𝒵 π \mathcal{Z}_{\pi} and a consistent estimator F ^ π TFEP \hat{F}_{\pi}^{\text{TFEP}} of F π F_{\pi} as N → ∞ N\to\infty . However, as for IS, it can suffer from large variance at finite N N if ρ θ \rho_{\theta} is not close enough to π \pi . The BAR method improves over TFEP in cases where samples from both ρ θ \rho_{\theta} and π \pi are available [ 15 ] . Given two sets of samples { x i } i = 1 N \{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} from ρ θ \rho_{\theta} and { x j } j = 1 M \{x_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M} from π \pi , the BAR estimator can be interpreted as the maximum likelihood estimate of the free energy difference obtained by viewing the problem as a binary classification task. The main ideas of the derivation (described in detail in appendix B ) are: given a sample x x , one asks whether it was drawn from ρ θ \rho_{\theta} or from π \pi . Using Bayes’ rule, the posterior probability that x x originates from ρ θ \rho_{\theta} can be written as a logistic function of the energy difference between the two models, involving the unknown free energy difference F π F_{\pi} . Maximizing the corresponding likelihood over the two sets of samples leads to a self-consistent equation whose solution defines the BAR estimator [ 158 ] . Namely, the estimator F ^ π BAR \hat{F}_{\pi}^{\text{BAR}} is defined as the solution of the implicit equation ∑ i = 1 N 1 1 + N M ​ e U ⁡ ( x i ) + log ⁡ ρ θ ​ ( x i ) − F ^ π BAR = ∑ j = 1 M 1 1 + M N ​ e − U ⁡ ( x j ) − log ⁡ ρ θ ​ ( x j ) + F ^ π BAR . \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{1+\frac{N}{M}e^{U(x_{i})+\log\rho_{\theta}(x_{i})-\hat{F}_{\pi}^{\text{BAR}}}}=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\frac{1}{1+\frac{M}{N}e^{-U(x_{j})-\log\rho_{\theta}(x_{j})+\hat{F}_{\pi}^{\text{BAR}}}}\;. (25) This estimator is known to be asymptotically optimal, meaning that, among estimators using samples from both distributions, it has minimal variance in the limit of infinite samples. A derivation specifically in the case of bijective mapping (relevant for NFs) is given in [ 74 ] . If BAR improves on TFEP, it strictly requires samples from the target distribution π \pi , which are not available a priori in the context discussed here. If some references use approximate samples obtained from molecular dynamics [ 48 ] , we note that provided an exact likelihood model approximating π \pi is available, the NF can also be used to converge an MCMC to generate samples from π \pi to be used in BAR [ 119 ] . The description of NF assisted MCMC schemes is precisely the topic of the next section.

sections.heading: 3.1.2 Independent proposal Markov chains
sections.text: MCMCs can also greatly benefit from an exact likelihood model trained to approximate the target distribution π \pi . A simple way to do so is to use the generative model as an independent proposal distribution in a Metropolis-Hastings (MH) algorithm [ 5 , 132 , 113 , 129 , 60 ] . The resulting algorithm reads: algorithm 2 flow/ARM independent Metropolis Hastings (flow-IMH/ARM-IMH) Initialize x ( 0 ) x^{(0)} , for k = 1 ​ … ​ K k=1\ldots K do Sample proposal x ′ ∼ ρ θ ​ ( ⋅ ) x^{\prime}\sim\rho_{\theta}(\cdot) , Compute acceptance probability α = min ⁡ ( 1 , π ⁡ ( x ′ ) π ⁡ ( x ( k − 1 ) ) × ρ θ ​ ( x ( k − 1 ) ) ρ θ ​ ( x ′ ) ) , \displaystyle\alpha=\min\left(1\,,\;\frac{\pi(x^{\prime})}{\pi(x^{(k-1)})}\times\frac{\rho_{\theta}(x^{(k-1)})}{\rho_{\theta}(x^{\prime})}\right)\,, Set x ( k ) = x ′ x^{(k)}=x^{\prime} with probability α \alpha , else x ( k ) = x ( k − 1 ) x^{(k)}=x^{(k-1)} , return samples { x ( k ) } k = 1 K \{x^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K} As in IS, observe that the proposal distribution of a MH algorithm needs to be (i) easy to sample from and (ii) its density needs to be tractable to evaluate the acceptance probability, both conditions being satisfied by NFs and ARMs. The resulting independent proposal MCMC is asymptotically unbiased regardless of the quality of the generative model approximation, meaning that the distribution of x ( K ) x^{(K)} converges to π \pi as K → ∞ K\to\infty . However, at finite K K , the acceptance rate of the algorithm directly depends on the agreement of ρ θ \rho_{\theta} with π \pi , being equal to 1 1 when ρ θ = π \rho_{\theta}=\pi and dropping to zero when ρ θ \rho_{\theta} is a poor approximation of π \pi . A high acceptance rate implies an extremely efficient sampler here as the proposal are global moves , uncorrelated with the current state of the chain. Attempting global moves across the state space is made possible by the flexibility of ARMs and NFs to approximate complex distributions, and represents a key advantage of using deep generative models as proposal distributions in place of local proposals such as random-walk or Langevin dynamics. In particular, global moves can help escape from metastable states in multimodal distributions, a situation where local MCMC proposals often fail.

sections.heading: Local-global Markov Chains
sections.text: Variants around the independent Metropolis-Hastings presented above can also be of interest. For instance, one can consider a hybrid scheme alternating local MCMC moves (e.g. Langevin dynamics or MH with Gaussian jump proposals, see appendix A for reminders on the local samplers used throughout this review) and global NF-based proposals [ 60 , 147 ] . This is particularly useful when the generative model misrepresents some part of the target distribution, as the local moves can help improve exploration in such regions. The advantage of alternating local and global moves was theoretically proven for simple statistical physics models [ 44 ] .

sections.heading: Multi-proposal version
sections.text: Another interesting variant considers more than one proposal per iteration [ 147 ] , following the iterated sampling importance resampling (iSIR) scheme [ 11 ] . Given the cheap sampling cost of NFs, one can consider M > 1 M>1 proposals { x i ′ } i = 1 M \{x^{\prime}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M} sampled from ρ θ \rho_{\theta} at each iteration of the MCMC yielding the following algorithm: algorithm 3 flow iterated sampling importance resampling (flow-iSIR) Initialize x ( 0 ) x^{(0)} , for k = 1 ​ … ​ K k=1\ldots K do Set x 0 ′ = x ( k − 1 ) x^{\prime}_{0}=x^{(k-1)} , for i = 1 ​ … ​ M i=1\ldots M do Sample proposal x i ′ ∼ ρ θ ​ ( ⋅ ) x^{\prime}_{i}\sim\rho_{\theta}(\cdot) , for i = 0 ​ … ​ M i=0\ldots M do Compute weight w i = π ⁡ ( x i ′ ) ρ θ ​ ( x i ′ ) w_{i}=\frac{\pi(x^{\prime}_{i})}{\rho_{\theta}(x^{\prime}_{i})} , for i = 0 ​ … ​ M i=0\ldots M do Compute normalized weight w ^ i = w i / ∑ j = 0 M w j \hat{w}_{i}=w_{i}/\sum_{j=0}^{M}w_{j} , Sample index i i from the categorical distribution with probabilities { w ^ j } j = 0 M \{\hat{w}_{j}\}_{j=0}^{M} , Set x ( k ) = x i ′ x^{(k)}=x^{\prime}_{i} , return samples { x ( k ) } k = 1 K \{x^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K} This approach was proposed using NFs but can readily be adapted for ARMs. By considering multiple proposals, this scheme increases the chance to propose a state in high probability regions of the target distribution, improving the mixing of the chain per iteration. However, the computational cost per iteration also increases with M M . As a result, a large M M is typically advantageous if parallel computing resources are available, even if the overall computational efficiency of the sampler does not necessarily improve with M M .

sections.heading: 3.1.3 Reparametrization through transport maps
sections.text: Yet another way to leverage NFs for sampling is to use them as reparametrization maps to simplify the geometry of the target distribution [ 136 , 81 , 132 , 24 , 155 ] . Here, we reference this set of methods as neutra-MCMCs following [ 81 ] play of words on neural transport maps "NeuTra-lizing" the target’s bad geometry. As this approach relies on the transport construction of NFs, it cannot be directly applied to ARMs. Recall that a NF is built from a base distribution ρ 0 \rho_{0} and a transport map T θ T_{\theta} . Once T θ T_{\theta} has been trained such that ρ θ \rho_{\theta} (given by eq. 4 ) approximates the target distribution π \pi is available, one can consider the pullback distribution of π \pi through T θ T_{\theta} defined as π T θ ​ ( z ) = π ⁡ ( T θ ​ ( z ) ) ​ | det ∇ z T θ ​ ( z ) | for ​ z ∈ 𝒳 . \displaystyle\pi_{T_{\theta}}(z)=\pi(T_{\theta}(z))\left|\det\nabla_{z}T_{\theta}(z)\right|\quad\text{for }z\in\mathcal{X}\;. (26) By construction, if ρ θ \rho_{\theta} is a good approximation of π \pi , then the pullback distribution π T θ \pi_{T_{\theta}} is close to the base distribution ρ 0 \rho_{0} , which is usually chosen to be a distribution with easy geometry (e.g. standard Gaussian). Sampling from π \pi can therefore be achieved by first sampling from the simpler distribution π T θ \pi_{T_{\theta}} and then pushing forward the samples through T θ T_{\theta} . For instance, if indeed ρ 0 = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) \rho_{0}=\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) , following the intuition that π T θ ≈ ρ 0 \pi_{T_{\theta}}\approx\rho_{0} , a natural choice is to resort to Langevin dynamics for sampling in the latent space, either with a Metropolis accept reject (MALA for Metropolis adjusted Langevin algorithm) or without (ULA for unadjusted Langevin algorithm). 4 4 4 See appendix A for reminders on these common local samplers. However, all other types of samplers can be employed: [ 81 ] examined Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), [ 24 ] elliptical slice sampling and [ 155 ] Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampling. Provided an unbiased sampler is used to target ρ 0 = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) \rho_{0}=\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) , transporting its output through T θ T_{\theta} provides unbiased samples from π \pi . Sketching an algorithm to summarize the overall method yields: algorithm 4 neutra-MCMC Initialize z ( 0 ) z^{(0)} , for k = 1 ​ … ​ K k=1\ldots K do z ( k + 1 ) ∼ M T θ , π ( ⋅ | z ( k ) ) z^{(k+1)}\sim M_{T_{\theta},\pi}(\cdot|z^{(k)}) with M T θ , π M_{T_{\theta},\pi} Markov kernel leaving π T θ \pi_{T_{\theta}} invariant, x ( k + 1 ) = T θ ​ ( z ( k + 1 ) ) x^{(k+1)}=T_{\theta}(z^{(k+1)}) return samples { x ( k ) } k = 1 K \{x^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K} Note that Markov kernels M T θ , π ( ⋅ | z ( k ) ) M_{T_{\theta},\pi}(\cdot|z^{(k)}) based on gradient information of the target distribution –such as MALA, ULA and HMC– require computing gradients of π T θ \pi_{T_{\theta}} at each iteration of the algorithm. This involves automatic differentiation through T θ T_{\theta} making each update significantly more costly than when directly targeting π \pi and hence the overall efficiency of the sampler is not guaranteed to improve. However, the advantage of neutra-MCMCs is that they can be more robust to ill-conditioning of the target distribution than standard MCMC methods, as we will discuss in section 3.2 .

sections.heading: 3.2 A first comparison of NF powered samplers
sections.text: Faced with the variety of ways of easing sampling leveraging a transport map T θ T_{\theta} sending ρ 0 \rho_{0} close to the target π \pi , a comparison is in order. A detailed numerical benchmark was conducted in [ 67 ] , considering different sources of difficulties in sampling, namely ill-conditioning, multimodality and high-dimensionality. We rediscuss the results of this study in the following paragraphs.

sections.heading: Neutra-MCMCs are the most robust to ill-conditioning
sections.text: If regions of high-probability of the target have significantly different scales in different directions of the state space, the target distribution is said to be ill-conditioned and this typically causes trouble to the convergence of MCMC based samplers. To assess the ability of the different flow-based approaches to alleviate this issue, one needs to also consider the quality of the training of T θ T_{\theta} . For a perfectly trained flow ρ θ = π \rho_{\theta}=\pi , and IS and IMH produce i.i.d samples from π \pi and are therefore optimal. The picture becomes more complicated if a residual mismatch persists between ρ θ \rho_{\theta} and π \pi . To systematically assess the effect of an imperfect learning on sampling an ill-conditioned target, the following experiment was conducted. The target distribution is a high-dimensional Gaussian ( d = 128 d=128 ) with an ill-conditioned covariance (see appendix D.2 of [ 67 ] for complete experimental setting). An analytical flow is defined with a scalar quality parameter t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] as illustrated on the left panel of fig. 1 . For t = 0.5 t=0.5 the flow is perfect. For t = 0 t=0 the flow density ρ t \rho_{t} is isotropic and over-concentrated, with variance matching the smallest directional variance of the target distribution. Conversely, for t = 1 t=1 , ρ t \rho_{t} is isotropic underconcentrated, matching the largest directional variance of the target distribution. When t ≠ 0.5 t\neq 0.5 , the flow fails at perfectly preconditioning the pullback π T t \pi_{T_{t}} . Results of the experiment reproduced on the right panel of fig. 1 show that neutra-MCMC methods are more robust to an imperfect map than approaches based on independent proposals (neural-IS, flow-IMH, flow-iSIR) whose performances degrade quickly as the flow training parameter deviates from t = 0.5 t=0.5 . This advantage is however mitigated with the cost per iteration of the method (higher than for independent proposal methods by a factor of 2 to 30 for the experiments reported in [ 67 ] ) and the challenges posed by multimodality for neutra-MCMCs, as discussed next. Figure 1 : (Left) Pullback π T t \pi_{T_{t}} and pushforward ρ t \rho_{t} as a function of the flow imperfection parameter t t . (Right) Sliced TV distances to target of NF-powered Monte Carlo samples compared as a function of the quality of the flow t t , using 256 chains of length 1400 initialized with draws from NF with T t T_{t} . neural-IS was evaluated with 14000 samples. Results were qualitatively unchanged for d = 16 , 32 , 64 , 256 d=16,32,64,256 . ESS stands for elliptical sliced-sampling in this figure. Reproduced from [ 67 ] .

sections.heading: Neutra-MCMCs struggle to mix between modes
sections.text: When the target π \pi is multimodal, the intuition that the pullback π T θ \pi_{T_{\theta}} has a simplified geometry breaks down. The reason is that common NF architecture based on transporting a standard Gaussian ρ \rho through coupling layers have troubles separating the mass of ρ 0 \rho_{0} into truly disconnected modes and respectively do not generate pullbacks with reunited mass. The difficulty of NFs to match multimodal distribution has been discussed in [ 38 , 146 ] . Figure 2 illustrates well this phenomenon on a 2 d d example. Figure 2 : Pullback and pushforward of popular deep normalizing flows architectures targeting the two moons distribution. Reproduced from [ 67 ] As a result, neutraMCMCs relying on MCMC kernels struggling with multimodality are not out of trouble by targeting the pullback. In this context, methods relying on independent proposals such as flow-IMH are better off. This can be seen on the results presented on the left and center panel of fig. 3 considering the task of sampling from a Gaussian mixture. In particular, as the dimension increases, methods based on reparametrization increasingly fail to discover all the modes of the distribution despite the fact that the pushfoward ρ θ \rho_{\theta} did have significant mass overlap with all the modes. However, this success of independent proposal methods for multimodal distribution is limited by their sensitivity as the dimension further increases, which we examine next. Figure 3 : (Left) Example chains of NF-enhanced walkers with a 2d target mixture of 4 Gaussians. The 128-step MCMC chain is colored according to the closest mode in the data space (bottom row) with corresponding location in the latent space (top row). The complex geometry of the pullback π T θ \pi_{T_{\theta}} hinders the mixing of local-update algorithms. MALA’s step-size was chosen to reach 75% of acceptance. (Middle) Median squared error of the histograms of visited modes of 4 Gaussians per chain against the perfect uniform histogram as a function of dimension. 512 chains of 1000-steps on average were used. (Right) Sliced total variation in sampling the Banana distribution in increasing dimension using a RealNVP. 128 chains of 1024-steps were used. Reproduced from [ 67 ]

sections.heading: Independent proposal methods are most affected by high-dimensionality
sections.text: Methods relying on independent proposals, either in the context of importance sampling (neural-IS) or of MCMCs (flow-IMH and flow-iSIR) suffer similarly from the increase of the dimensionality. A classical elementary calculation by [ 2 ] allows to catch the source of the difficulty considering the example case where the considered target and proposal distributions are the product of 1 d d measures. But before we cover this example, let us define an important quantity to assess the efficiency of IS and IMH that has not yet been introduced. The effective sample size (ESS) [ 98 ] is defined, for a batch of N N samples { x i } i = 1 N \{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} drawn from the proposal distribution ρ \rho , with importance weights w ⁡ ( x i ) = π ⁡ ( x i ) / ρ ⁡ ( x i ) w(x_{i})=\pi(x_{i})/\rho(x_{i}) , as ESS = ( ∑ i = 1 N w ⁡ ( x i ) ) 2 ∑ i = 1 N w ​ ( x i ) 2 . \displaystyle\text{ESS}=\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}w(x_{i})\right)^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N}w(x_{i})^{2}}. (27) If all the weights are equal, meaning that the proposal perfectly matches the target, then ESS = N \text{ESS}=N . Conversely, if one weight dominates all the others, then ESS ≈ 1 \text{ESS}\approx 1 . The ESS therefore provides a measure of the number of independent samples from the target distribution that can be extracted from the weighted samples drawn from the proposal. Note that both unormalized and self-normalized IS weights can be used to compute the ESS, as the normalization constant cancels out in the ratio. Going back to the example of product of 1 d d distributions, consider target and proposal distributions defined on 𝒳 = ℝ d \mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^{d} as π ⁡ ( x ) = ∏ i = 1 d π 1 ​ d ​ ( x i ) ​ and ​ ρ ​ ( x ) = ∏ i = 1 d ρ 1 ​ d ​ ( x i ) . \displaystyle\pi(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{d}\pi_{1d}(x_{i})\;\text{ and }\;\rho(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{d}\rho_{1d}(x_{i}). (28) Then the importance weight function itself factorizes w ⁡ ( x ) = ∏ i = 1 d w 1 ​ d ​ ( x i ) w(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{d}w_{1d}(x_{i}) with w 1 ​ d ​ ( x i ) = π 1 ​ d ​ ( x i ) / ρ 1 ​ d ​ ( x i ) w_{1d}(x_{i})=\pi_{1d}(x_{i})/\rho_{1d}(x_{i}) . In the limit of large N N , thanks to the independence of all the coordinates, the ESS can be approximated as ESS ≈ ( N ​ 𝔼 ρ ​ [ w 1 ​ d ] d ) 2 N ​ 𝔼 ρ ​ [ w 1 ​ d 2 ] d = N ​ ( 𝔼 ρ 1 ​ d ​ [ w 1 ​ d ] 2 𝔼 ρ 1 ​ d ​ [ w 1 ​ d 2 ] ) d ≈ N ​ e − d ​ log ⁡ ( 𝔼 ρ 1 ​ d ​ [ w 1 ​ d ] 2 / 𝔼 ρ 1 ​ d ​ [ w 1 ​ d 2 ] ) \displaystyle\text{ESS}\approx\frac{(N\mathbb{E}_{\rho}[w_{1d}]^{d})^{2}}{N\mathbb{E}_{\rho}[w_{1d}^{2}]^{d}}=N\left(\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{1d}}[w_{1d}]^{2}}{\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{1d}}[w_{1d}^{2}]}\right)^{d}\approx Ne^{-d\log\left(\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{1d}}[w_{1d}]^{2}/\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{1d}}[w_{1d}^{2}]\right)}\, (29) where the logarithm in the exponent is positive unless the proposal perfectly matches the target in 1 d d in which case it is zero. This calculation shows that unless a perfect match is achieved, the ESS decays exponentially fast with the dimension d d . Although this calculation is made under restrictive assumptions, it captures well the curse of dimensionality affecting IS and IMH methods. For instance, note that in statistical mechanics applications of sampling, the target distribution takes the form of a Boltzmann-Gibbs distribution π ⁡ ( x ) ∝ e − U ⁡ ( x ) \pi(x)\propto e^{-U(x)} where the potential energy U ⁡ ( x ) U(x) is often extensive in the number of degrees of freedom, meaning scaling linearly with d d . In such situations, even small relative errors in the approximation of U ⁡ ( x ) U(x) by the NF transport map T θ T_{\theta} can lead to exponentially small ESS as d d increases. The right panel of fig. 3 illustrates this curse of dimensionality affecting independent proposal methods, considering the task of sampling from a banana-shaped distribution in increasing dimension. Similar results have been reported by other works from which the systematic study of [ 45 ] stands out. This work focuses on sampling from the Boltzmann distribution of a lattice field theory, the 2d ϕ 4 \phi^{4} model, of which the size of the lattice directly controls the dimension of the state space. Additionally, a temperature parameter controls the difficulty of the sampling task, the model going through a phase transition where the correlation length between lattice sites diverges, making the sampling particularly challenging. Despite an extensive hyperparameter search and the use of advanced NF architectures, the authors find that the acceptance rate of flow-IMH samplers decreases invariably as the lattice size increases and as the temperature approaches the critical point.

sections.heading: Where do the elementary NF enhanced samplers stand?
sections.text: Summarizing the above discussion, we can sketch the state of affairs after initial research efforts on leveraging NFs for sampling. Independent proposal methods such as neural-IS and flow-IMH are well suited for sampling multimodal distributions thanks to their ability to explore globally the state space. However, they suffer from the curse of dimensionality, with performances degrading quickly as the dimension of the state space increases, unless a near perfect flow approximation is available. To provide an order of magnitude, the highest dimension admissible for independent proposals lies somewhere between a hundred to a few thousands depending on the regularity of the target distribution. This range covers many practical applications such as Bayesian inference for medium size models or molecular systems with a few tens of atoms, but falls short for larger applications such as simulating liquids, large biomolecules or statistical mechanics field theories toward the continuum limit. Conversely, neutra-MCMCs leveraging local samplers in the latent space are more robust to high-dimensional settings and ill-conditioning. However, they struggle to mix between modes when the target distribution is multimodal, as the pullback distribution often retains a complex geometry hindering the convergence of local samplers. Taken together, these observations motivate the development of more advanced NF-powered samplers that leverage modern advances in the sampling literature, which has progressed considerably beyond the elementary tools of IS and MH. In the next two sections we review how NF can be combined with the ideas of annealing and of exploiting coarse-grainings to enhance sampling. While some of the methods covered next can be adapted to ARMs, many of them rely on the transport construction of NFs and we therefore focus on NFs in the following sections.

sections.heading: 3.3 Combining NFs with tempering
sections.text: Recall that annealed based samplers, such as annealed importance sampling (AIS), parallel tempering (PT) and sequential Monte Carlo (SMC), already mentioned in the introduction, rely on a bridging path between a simple reference measure and the target measure. The philosophy behind combining tempering with NFs is no longer to expect that a single NF transport map directly reaches the target distribution, but instead to delegate part of the sampling effort to tempering-based schemes. Below, we highlight several key examples, without attempting an exhaustive survey given the rapid pace of recent developments in the literature.

sections.heading: 3.3.1 Adapting the base distribution to the target
sections.text: A first step in the direction of tempering is to adapt the base distribution ρ 0 \rho_{0} of the NF to be closer to the target distribution π \pi , easing the training of the NF and improving its final accuracy. The choice of ρ 0 \rho_{0} is highly task dependent as it needs to remain relatively easy to sample. The idea was used on statistical physics fields systems using a Gaussian base with matching small scale correlations [ 61 ] , in sampling liquids using a less dense and/or higher temperature fluid as base [ 151 , 93 , 36 ] , as well as for sampling crystals and materials using Einstein’s harmonic crystal as base [ 177 , 179 , 152 ] . This is a natural way to incorporate physics knowledge into NF-based sampling schemes that can considerably ease the learning task. It can be further combined with tempering schemes described next.

sections.heading: 3.3.2 Combining NFs with AIS: stochastic normalizing flows
sections.text: [ 185 ] introduced a stochastic type of NFs amenable to enhanced sampling using the AIS framework. Instead of relying on a deterministic transport map T θ T_{\theta} , the flow alternates deterministic NF layers and stochastic Markovian layers. The advantage of stochastic NFs lies in the ability of stochastic layers to represent a multimodal target distribution given an unimodal base distribution ρ 0 \rho_{0} , which traditional deterministic coupling layers struggle to achieve. A stochastic NF with L L layers is defined as a sequence of random variables ( x 0 , … , x L ) (x^{0},\dots,x^{L}) with x 0 ∼ ρ 0 x^{0}\sim\rho_{0} and x L x^{L} being the output of the flow. The transition from layer ℓ − 1 \ell-1 to layer ℓ \ell is defined by a transition kernel q θ ℓ ​ ( x ℓ | x ℓ − 1 ) q_{\theta_{\ell}}(x^{\ell}|x^{\ell-1}) parametrized by θ ℓ \theta_{\ell} . Deterministic NF layers are implemented via a bijective map T θ ℓ T_{\theta_{\ell}} such that q θ ℓ ​ ( x ℓ | x ℓ − 1 ) = δ ⁡ ( x ℓ − T θ ℓ ​ ( x ℓ − 1 ) ) q_{\theta_{\ell}}(x^{\ell}|x^{\ell-1})=\delta(x^{\ell}-T_{\theta_{\ell}}(x^{\ell-1})) . Stochastic layers are characterized through a q θ ℓ ​ ( x ℓ | x ℓ − 1 ) q_{\theta_{\ell}}(x^{\ell}|x^{\ell-1}) with explicit probability density and easy to sample from. The overall joint probability density over ( x 0 , … , x L ) (x_{0},\dots,x_{L}) and the marginal output distribution read respectively: ρ θ ​ ( x 0 , … , x L ) = ρ 0 ​ ( x 0 ) ​ ∏ ℓ = 1 L q θ ℓ ​ ( x ℓ | x ℓ − 1 ) , ρ θ ​ ( x L ) = ∫ ∏ ℓ = 0 L − 1 d ​ x ℓ ​ ρ θ ​ ( x 0 , … , x L ) . \displaystyle\rho_{\theta}(x^{0},\dots,x^{L})=\rho_{0}(x^{0})\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}q_{\theta_{\ell}}(x^{\ell}|x^{\ell-1}),\;\quad\rho_{\theta}(x^{L})=\int\prod_{\ell=0}^{L-1}dx^{\ell}\,\rho_{\theta}(x^{0},\dots,x^{L}). (30) The marginal output distribution ρ θ ​ ( x L ) \rho_{\theta}(x^{L}) is intractable as it involves marginalizing over all stochastic layers. As such, proposals from the stochastic NF cannot be used directly in Neural-IS ( algorithm 1 ) or flow-IMH ( algorithm 2 ) to estimate expectations under the target distribution π \pi . Resorting instead to AIS-like scheme, a set of backward transition kernels needs to be introduced. The backward kernels, with parameters θ ~ ℓ \tilde{\theta}_{\ell} , are denoted by q ~ θ ~ ℓ ​ ( x ℓ − 1 | x ℓ ) \tilde{q}_{\tilde{\theta}_{\ell}}(x^{\ell-1}|x^{\ell}) and allow to define a backward joint distribution with π \pi as last marginal: ρ ~ θ ~ ​ ( x 0 , … , x L ) = π ⁡ ( x L ) ​ ∏ ℓ = 1 L q ~ θ ~ ℓ ​ ( x ℓ − 1 | x ℓ ) , π ⁡ ( x L ) = ∫ ∏ ℓ = 1 L d ​ x ℓ − 1 ​ ρ ~ θ ~ ​ ( x 0 , … , x L ) . \displaystyle\tilde{\rho}_{\tilde{\theta}}(x^{0},\dots,x^{L})=\pi(x^{L})\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\tilde{q}_{\tilde{\theta}_{\ell}}(x^{\ell-1}|x^{\ell}),\quad\pi(x^{L})=\int\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}dx^{\ell-1}\,\tilde{\rho}_{\tilde{\theta}}(x^{0},\dots,x^{L})\;. (31) An importance sampling estimator is constructed at the level of the joint distributions based on the equality 𝔼 π ​ [ f ⁡ ( x ) ] = 𝔼 ρ θ ​ [ f ⁡ ( x L ) × w ⁡ ( x 0 , … , x L ) ] , with ​ w ​ ( x 0 , … , x L ) = ρ ~ θ ~ ​ ( x 0 , … , x L ) ρ θ ​ ( x 0 , … , x L ) , \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[f(x)]=\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{\theta}}\left[f(x^{L})\times w(x^{0},\dots,x^{L})\right],\quad\text{with }w(x^{0},\dots,x^{L})=\frac{\tilde{\rho}_{\tilde{\theta}}(x^{0},\dots,x^{L})}{\rho_{\theta}(x^{0},\dots,x^{L})}\;, (32) for any test function f : 𝒳 → ℝ f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} . The resulting self-normalized importance sampling estimator of 𝔼 π ​ [ f ​ ( x ) ] \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[f(x)] reads f ^ SNF = ∑ i = 1 N f ⁡ ( x i L ) ​ w ​ ( x i 0 , … , x i L ) ∑ i = 1 N w ⁡ ( x i 0 , … , x i L ) with ​ ( x i 0 , … , x i L ) ∼ ρ θ ​ ( ⋅ ) . \displaystyle\hat{f}_{\text{SNF}}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}f(x^{L}_{i})\,w(x^{0}_{i},\dots,x^{L}_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{N}w(x^{0}_{i},\dots,x^{L}_{i})}\quad\text{with }(x^{0}_{i},\dots,x^{L}_{i})\sim\rho_{\theta}(\cdot)\;. (33) The efficiency of the resulting estimator relies on the agreement between the forward and backward joint distributions ρ θ \rho_{\theta} and ρ ~ θ ~ \tilde{\rho}_{\tilde{\theta}} , which in turn depends on the specification of the forward and backward kernels. In practice, [ 185 ] suggests designing deterministic and stochastic layers such that the marginal distributions at the successive layers follow as closely as possible an interpolation path between the base distribution ρ 0 \rho_{0} and the target distribution π \pi (e.g. π ℓ = ρ 0 ( L − ℓ ) / L ​ π ℓ / L \pi_{\ell}=\rho_{0}^{(L-\ell)/L}\pi^{{\ell/L}} ), as traditionally done in AIS. This approach has also strong connections with non-equilibrium statistical mechanics equalities by Jarzynski and Crooks [ 88 , 41 ] , and their repurposing for Monte Carlo [ 130 ] . The advantage of learning NF layers on top of vanilla non-equilibrium Monte Carlo moves was validated in particular in high-energy physics applications [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] . In the next section, we discuss a very related line of work combining NFs with SMC.

sections.heading: 3.3.3 Combining NFs with SMC
sections.text: The additional ingredient of SMC methods compared to AIS is the intermediate resampling among parallel draws (referred to as particles). For this, SMC relies on a sequence of intermediate distributions ( π ℓ ) ℓ = 0 L \left(\pi_{\ell}\right)_{\ell=0}^{L} with π 0 = ρ 0 \pi_{0}=\rho_{0} and π L = π \pi_{L}=\pi and π ℓ = e − U ℓ / Z ℓ \pi_{\ell}=e^{-U_{\ell}}/Z_{\ell} . The resampling steps aim at guaranteeing a good agreement between the distribution of the particles and the current target distribution π ℓ \pi_{\ell} . Combining SMC with NFs, [ 12 , 112 ] assume to have a set of transport maps ( T θ ℓ ) ℓ = 1 L \left(T_{\theta_{\ell}}\right)_{\ell=1}^{L} respectively trained to approximately transport π ℓ \pi_{\ell} to π ℓ + 1 \pi_{\ell+1} . The SMC procedures then combines these maps, with the standard SMC steps of mutation, weighting and resampling. The algorithm can be summarized as follows: algorithm 5 (Continuously Repeated) Annealed Flow Transport (AFT/CRAFT) Initialize particles { x i ( 0 ) } i = 1 N ∼ π 0
