kernel, return particles { x i ( L ) } i = 1 N \{x_{i}^{(L)}\}_{i=1}^{N} and normalization constant estimate 𝒵 ^ L \hat{\mathcal{Z}}_{L} . As is now common practice in SMC, the resampling step is triggered only when the effective sample size (ESS) drops below a threshold α \alpha (e.g. α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 ). Also note that the method allows to estimate the normalizing constant of the target distribution π \pi as a by-product (which is also the case for AIS but was omitted in the previous section for brevity). By dividing the task of sampling from π \pi into smaller subtasks of sampling sequentially from successive intermediate distributions π ℓ \pi_{\ell} , AFT/CRAFT eases the learning of each transport map T θ ℓ T_{\theta_{\ell}} compared to elementary NF-powered samplers. Additionally, the resampling step helps focus computational efforts on particles in high probability regions of the target distribution, which is particularly useful when the target is multimodal. Finally, the mutation step relying on local MCMC kernels M ℓ M_{\ell} helps improve the diversity of the particles and correct for residual errors in the flow approximations. While combining all these ingredients increases the computational cost of the sampler compared to flow-IMH or Neural-IS, it also logically improves its robustness to challenging sampling tasks. Compared to regular SMC, the addition of transport maps allows to use a coarser interpolation ladder: the requirement that π ℓ − 1 \pi_{\ell-1} and π ℓ \pi_{\ell} be close enough, to avoid weights degeneracy, becomes that the pushforward of π ℓ − 1 \pi_{\ell-1} through T ℓ T_{\ell} be close enough to π ℓ \pi_{\ell} . As a result, fewer intermediate steps are necessary to reach a good sampling performance. In a related proposition, [ 94 ] combines NFs with SMC using a single transport map that is trained progressively to transport the base distribution ρ 0 \rho_{0} to the current intermediate target π ℓ \pi_{\ell} at each iteration of SMC. In this work, the mutation step takes also advantage of the NF transport map to employ a neutra-MCMC kernel as described in algorithm 4 . The performance of this approach was validated on cosmological and astronomical Bayesian inference tasks.

sections.heading: 3.3.4 Combining NFs with PT
sections.text: Following the propositions made for AIS and SMC, NFs can also be used to ease sampling in the PT framework. As a reminder PT relies on a similar interpolation path ( x ℓ ) ℓ = 0 L \left(x_{\ell}\right)_{\ell=0}^{L} and consists in simulating in parallel a set of L + 1 L+1 replicas ( x ℓ ) ℓ = 0 L \left(x_{\ell}\right)_{\ell=0}^{L} sampling respectively from the intermediate distribution π ℓ \pi_{\ell} . Periodic swaps are proposed between replicas at adjacent levels ℓ \ell and ℓ + 1 \ell+1 . To ensure a reasonable acceptance rate for swap proposals, neighboring distributions π ℓ \pi_{\ell} and π ℓ + 1 \pi_{\ell+1} must be close enough, which often leads to the necessity of maintaining many replicas at high computational cost. In this context, [ 87 ] proposed to leverage NFs to skip all the intermediate steps altogether. The idea is to approximately transport an easy replica x 0 x_{0} sampling from π 0 = ρ 0 \pi_{0}=\rho_{0} to the target π L = π \pi_{L}=\pi while transporting a target replica x L x_{L} to ρ 0 \rho_{0} , before attempting their swap. Thereby, only two replicas are strictly necessary. Following standard practice in PT, the base distribution is typically adapted to the target distribution, choosing π 0 ∝ π β \pi_{0}\propto\pi^{\beta} , with β < 1 \beta<1 , a high-temperature version of the target distribution π \pi . As a result, ρ 0 = π 0 \rho_{0}=\pi_{0} is not as trivial to sample from than when choosing a standard Gaussian, but the assumption is that a local MCMC sampler can still efficiently explore π 0 \pi_{0} . Denoting by T θ T_{\theta} a NF transport map trained to transport ρ 0 \rho_{0} to π \pi , and M 0 M_{0} and M π M_{\pi} local Markov kernels leaving respectively ρ 0 \rho_{0} and π \pi invariant, the PT procedure is modified as follows: algorithm 6 Learned replica exchange (LREX) Initialize replicas x 0 ( 0 ) x_{0}^{(0)} and x π ( 0 ) x_{\pi}^{(0)} at random, for k=1…K do x 0 ( k ) ∼ M 0 ( ⋅ | x 0 ( k − 1 ) ) x_{0}^{(k)}\sim M_{0}(\cdot|x_{0}^{(k-1)}) , x π ( k ) ∼ M π ( ⋅ | x π ( k − 1 ) ) x_{\pi}^{(k)}\sim M_{\pi}(\cdot|x_{\pi}^{(k-1)}) , Draw u ∼ Uniform ​ ( 0 , 1 ) u\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1) if u < γ u<\gamma then Attempt swap: x 0 ′ = T θ − 1 ​ ( x π ( k ) ) x_{0}^{\prime}=T_{\theta}^{-1}(x_{\pi}^{(k)}) x π ′ = T θ ​ ( x 0 ( k ) ) x_{\pi}^{\prime}=T_{\theta}(x_{0}^{(k)}) , Compute α = min ⁡ ( 1 , π ⁡ ( x π ′ ) ​ ρ θ ​ ( T θ ​ ( x 0 ′ ) ) π ⁡ ( x π ( k ) ) ​ ρ θ ​ ( T θ ​ ( x 0 ( k ) ) ) ) = min ⁡ ( 1 , π ⁡ ( x π ′ ) ​ ρ 0 ​ ( x 0 ′ ) π ⁡ ( x π ( k ) ) ​ ρ 0 ​ ( x 0 ( k ) ) × | det ∇ T θ ​ ( x 0 ( k ) ) det ∇ T θ ​ ( x 0 ′ ) | ) \alpha=\min\left(1,\frac{\pi(x_{\pi}^{\prime})\rho_{\theta}(T_{\theta}(x_{0}^{\prime}))}{\pi(x_{\pi}^{(k)})\rho_{\theta}(T_{\theta}(x_{0}^{(k)}))}\right)=\min\left(1,\frac{\pi(x_{\pi}^{\prime})\rho_{0}(x_{0}^{\prime})}{\pi(x_{\pi}^{(k)})\rho_{0}(x_{0}^{(k)})}\times\left|\frac{\det\nabla T_{\theta}(x_{0}^{(k)})}{\det\nabla T_{\theta}(x_{0}^{\prime})}\right|\,\right) , Set x 0 ( k ) ← x 0 ′ x_{0}^{(k)}\leftarrow x_{0}^{\prime} , x π ( k ) ← x π ′ x_{\pi}^{(k)}\leftarrow x_{\pi}^{\prime} with probability α \alpha The swap is attempted with probability γ \gamma at each iteration and ρ θ \rho_{\theta} denotes the density of the pushforward distribution induced by T θ T_{\theta} , given by the change-of-variables formula ( eq. 4 ). The acceptance probability α \alpha ensures that the overall Markov chain over the joint state space of the two replicas leaves the joint distribution ρ ⁡ ( x 0 , x π ) = ρ 0 ​ ( x 0 ) ​ π ​ ( x π ) \rho(x_{0},x_{\pi})=\rho_{0}(x_{0})\pi(x_{\pi}) invariant. In spirit, the proposition of [ 87 ] is similar to flow-IMH ( algorithm 2 ) except that the base distribution is not sampled independently and the non-local moves are mediated by swaps between the base and target replicas. As a result, one can expect similar performances of this approach compared to flow-IMH. A subsequent proposal by [ 188 ] places weaker requirements on the NF and retains a ladder of intermediate distributions ( π ℓ ) ℓ = 1 L \left(\pi_{\ell}\right)_{\ell=1}^{L} . As in SMC-based (CR)AFT, this ladder can be chosen coarser than in traditional PT, thanks to a collection of transport maps ( T ℓ ) ℓ = 1 L \left(T_{\ell}\right)_{\ell=1}^{L} that approximately push forward π ℓ − 1 \pi_{\ell-1} to π ℓ \pi_{\ell} . Extending the two-replica version of algorithm 6 , local MCMC kernels M ℓ M_{\ell} targeting each π ℓ \pi_{\ell} are run for every replica x ℓ x_{\ell} , and swaps between neighboring levels are periodically proposed using the corresponding transport maps. Although this strategy requires maintaining more replicas, it is expected to handle more complex target distributions than the two-replica scheme, as it decomposes the global transport from ρ \rho to π \pi into a sequence of simpler transitions from π ℓ − 1 \pi_{\ell-1} to π ℓ \pi_{\ell} .

sections.heading: 3.3.5 Recalibrating NF samples with AIS or SMC
sections.text: Returning to the setting where a single transport map T θ T_{\theta} is trained to push forward ρ 0 \rho_{0} to π \pi , it has also been proposed to leverage AIS or SMC in order to recalibrate the NF samples. The idea is to introduce a sequence of intermediate distributions that, here, gradually transports ρ θ \rho_{\theta} to π \pi , for instance π ℓ = ρ θ ( L − ℓ ) / L ​ π ℓ / L \pi_{\ell}=\rho_{\theta}^{(L-\ell)/L}\pi^{\ell/L} . Then, an AIS or SMC procedure is run targeting π \pi , initialized from samples drawn from ρ θ \rho_{\theta} . This strategy was first proposed by [ 116 ] in the context of AIS and more recently revisited by [ 167 ] using SMC. In contrast to elementary NF-based samplers, this approach explicitly compensates for imperfections in the learned transport map. In particular, since ρ θ \rho_{\theta} may not be sufficiently close to π \pi to serve directly as a proposal distribution for IS or IMH, the tempering procedure corrects for this mismatch. As with other combinations of tempering and normalizing flows, the computational cost is higher than that of flow-IMH or Neural-IS, but this additional effort is expected to translate into improved sampling performance. Although other innovations are presented in [ 116 ] and [ 167 ] , the former reports good performance of the AIS recalibration strategy on sampling from the Boltzmann measure of clusters of repulsive particles and the latter validates the SMC recalibration strategy on the sampling of small biomolecules. Intermediate summary Overall, the various proposals for combining NFs with tempering-based sampling schemes expand the capabilities of traditional tempering methods and ease the learning burden compared to the simple NF-powered samplers discussed above. However, a systematic comparison of these algorithms is still lacking. Moreover, while these approaches typically moderate the demands placed on learning—and are therefore likely to handle more complex targets than simple NF-enhanced samplers—it remains unclear whether they exhibit more favorable scaling with dimension. Indeed, transport is still performed in the full ambient space. The alternative strategy introduced next addresses this limitation directly by reducing the effective dimensionality of the problem.

sections.heading: 3.4 Combining NFs with coarse-grainings
sections.text: One emerging limitation of samplers relying on NF-based proposals is their poor scaling with dimension. Expecting a generative model to learn how to resample an entire high-dimensional variable in a coherent manner is, in a sense, overly ambitious. This observation motivates another line of research seeking to leverage NFs while avoiding a full resampling. This is the underlying principle of the two methods described below.

sections.heading: 3.4.1 Partial resampling in the latent space
sections.text: A first strategy to mitigate the deterioration of acceptance rates with increasing dimension is to perform partial updates informed by the generative model trained to approximate π \pi . With autoregressive models, this operation is straightforward provided that one updates variables appearing last in the autoregressive ordering [ 183 ] . However, in phases with strong correlations, updating a finite number of variables at the end of the ordering may not be sufficient to connect distant modes of the target distribution. In this context, [ 155 ] proposed an adaptation of this idea exploiting the latent space of a normalizing flow (with base distribution ρ 0 \rho_{0} and transport map T θ T_{\theta} ) where the variables are less correlated. The method, referred to as Gibbs flow-Monte Carlo (GFlowMC), uses a Metropolis-within-Gibbs scheme on the pullback π T θ \pi_{T_{\theta}} of π \pi through T θ T_{\theta} (see eq. 26 ) using the conditional distributions of ρ 0 \rho_{0} as proposal distributions, and subsequently accepting or rejecting the proposal according to a Metropolis acceptance rule. More precisely, let d u ≤ d d_{u}\leq d denote the number of degrees of freedom to be updated, S = ( i 1 , … , i d u ) S=(i_{1},\dots,i_{d_{u}}) a selected set of distinct indices, and q ⁡ ( S ) q(S) a probability distribution over such subsets. Denote by z S z_{S} and z ∖ S z_{\setminus S} the components of the base variable z z indexed by S S and by its complement, respectively. The partial resampling MCMC procedure of [ 155 ] consists in: algorithm 7 Gibbs flow-Monte Carlo (GflowMC) Initialize x ( 0 ) x^{(0)} , Compute z ( 0 ) = T θ − 1 ​ ( x ( 0 ) ) z^{(0)}=T_{\theta}^{-1}(x^{(0)}) , for k = 1 ​ … ​ K k=1\ldots K do Sample set S ∼ q ⁡ ( S ) S\sim q(S) , Propose partial refreshing z S ′ ∼ ρ 0 ​ ( z S | z ∖ S ( k − 1 ) ) z_{S}^{\prime}\sim\rho_{0}(z_{S}|z^{(k-1)}_{\setminus S}) , Set z ∖ S ′ = z ∖ S ( k − 1 ) z^{\prime}_{\setminus S}=z^{(k-1)}_{\setminus S} , Compute acceptance rate α = min ⁡ ( 1 , π T θ ​ ( z ′ ) π T θ ​ ( z ( k − 1 ) ) × ρ 0 ​ ( z S | z ∖ S ( k − 1 ) ) ρ 0 ​ ( z S ′ | z ∖ S ( k − 1 ) ) ) , \displaystyle\alpha=\min\left(1\,,\;\frac{\pi_{T_{\theta}}(z^{\prime})}{\pi_{T_{\theta}}(z^{(k-1)})}\times\frac{\rho_{0}(z_{S}|z^{(k-1)}_{\setminus S})}{\rho_{0}(z_{S}^{\prime}|z^{(k-1)}_{\setminus S})}\right)\,, Set z ( k ) = z ′ z^{(k)}=z^{\prime} with probability α \alpha , else z ( k ) = z ( k − 1 ) z^{(k)}=z^{(k-1)} , return samples { x ( k ) = T θ ( z ( k ) ) } k = 1 K \{x^{(k)}=T_{\theta}(z^{(k)})\}_{k=1}^{K} Here the density of the pullback π T θ \pi_{T_{\theta}} is again needed in the acceptance ratio. The conditional base distributions of the form ρ 0 ​ ( z S | z ∖ S ) \rho_{0}(z_{S}|z_{\setminus S}) are assumed to be explicit and easy to sample from. For a factorized ρ 0 \rho_{0} , this is trivially the case as the conditional distribution ρ 0 ​ ( z S | z ∖ S ) \rho_{0}(z_{S}|z_{\setminus S}) is equal to the marginal ρ 0 ​ ( z S ) \rho_{0}(z_{S}) , itself factorized – e.g. for the common choice ρ 0 = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 d , I d ) \rho_{0}=\mathcal{N}(0_{d},I_{d}) , ρ 0 ​ ( z S | z ∖ S ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 d u , I d u ) \rho_{0}(z_{S}|z_{\setminus S})=\mathcal{N}(0_{d_{u}},I_{d_{u}}) . The algorithm shares similarities with neutra-MCMC ( algorithm 4 ), but replaces the local MCMC updates in the latent space with partial global updates that can more easily jump across modes, as illustrated by the two-dimensional example in fig. 4 . In the context of statistical field theories, [ 155 ] report that GFlowMC can outperform both neutra-MCMC and flow-IMH. In particular, the number of degrees of freedom updated, d u d_{u} , acts as a tunable parameter for optimizing sampler performance by trading off acceptance rate against the decorrelation in a single move. Figure 4 : Illustration of the Gibbs flow-Monte Carlo (GFlowMC) algorithm. The target distribution π \pi is a mixture of two Gaussians (left pannel). The NF inverse transport map T θ − 1 T_{\theta}^{-1} approximately transports π \pi to a standard Gaussian base distribution ρ 0 \rho_{0} (middle left panel). The GFlowMC algorithm (middle right panel) performs partial resampling in the latent space of the NF targetting the pullback π T θ \pi_{T_{\theta}} (in orange), here updating one variable at a time ( d u = 1 d_{u}=1 ). Sending the samples back to the original space (right panel) evidence the ability of GFlowMC to jump between the two modes of π \pi . Adapted from the poster of C. Schönle on [ 155 ] . In an application to biomolecular systems, [ 137 ] exploit a similar idea using continuous normalizing flows (CNFs). They report that updating a single latent variable at a time ( d u = 1 d_{u}=1 ) is optimal, and demonstrate a significant acceleration in equilibrating samples of the small, fast-folding protein Chignolin. In the strategy described in the above paragraphs, the NF is still trained to approximate the full target distribution π \pi . An alternative approach consists in leveraging generative models to sample a low-dimensional coarse-grained representation of the system, which is the idea developed next.

sections.heading: 3.4.2 Collective-variable guided sampling
sections.text: As already mentioned in the introduction, apart from annealing-based methods, another key strategy to address metastability in high dimension relies on the existence of a low-dimensional representation (or coarse-graining), referred to as collective variables (CVs), that effectively separates the different modes of the target measure. In this context, generative models provide a flexible and scalable framework to estimate the marginal law of the CVs. In contrast to traditional non-parametric approaches — which typically restrict CV-guided algorithms to very low-dimensional CV spaces due to the difficulty of in keeping track of their marginal density — generative models make it possible to handle significantly higher-dimensional CV spaces. Generative models therefore extend the range of admissible dimensions for the CV representation in coarse-graining-based sampling strategies. Here, we review the approach proposed by [ 166 , 153 , 154 ] , revisiting the concept of CV-guided sampling using a NF trained to sample the distribution of the CVs. The approach is based on non-equilibrium samplers previously introduced without resorting to NFs, notably in [ 124 , 14 , 130 , 32 ] . For simplicity, we discuss the separable case where the CVs are a subset of the full variables, i.e. x = ( z , x ⟂ ) ∈ ℝ d x=(z,x^{\perp})\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , with z ∈ ℝ d z z\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} the CVs and x ⟂ ∈ ℝ d − d z x^{\perp}\in\mathbb{R}^{d-d_{z}} the remaining degrees of freedom. The strategy presented below readily generalizes to an arbitrary CV mapping z = ξ ⁡ ( x ) z=\xi(x) following [ 154 ] . In the separable case, the marginal distribution over CVs of the target distribution π ⁡ ( x ) \pi(x) is given by π z ​ ( z ) = ∫ π ⁡ ( z , x ⟂ ) ​ d ​ x ⟂ . \displaystyle\pi_{z}(z)=\int\pi(z,x^{\perp})\,dx^{\perp}\,. (34) The sampling algorithm then relies on two main ingredients: (i) a NF trained to sample approximately from the marginal distribution of the CVs, its probability density function is noted ρ θ ​ ( z ) \rho_{\theta}(z) , (ii) a non-equilibrium sampling procedure updating the value of x ⟂ x^{\perp} conditional on an updated value of the CVs z z . Let us describe the second ingredient. Given the current state x = ( z , x ⟂ ) x=(z,x^{\perp}) and a proposed new value z ′ z^{\prime} for the CVs, we introduce a T T -step path S ⁡ ( z , z ′ ) = ( z t ) t = 0 T S(z,z^{\prime})=(z_{t})_{t=0}^{T} connecting z z to z ′ z^{\prime} , with z 0 = z z_{0}=z and z T = z ′ z_{T}=z^{\prime} . A simple choice is the linear interpolation z t = z + ( z ′ − z ) ​ t / T z_{t}=z+(z^{\prime}-z)\,t/T . Starting from x 0 ⟂ = x ⟂ x_{0}^{\perp}=x^{\perp} , the orthogonal degrees of freedom are then updated through a sequence of T T Markov kernels associated with the intermediate values z t z_{t} : algorithm 8 Non-equilibrium update of orthogonal degrees of freedom Input: Current state x = ( z , x ⟂ ) x=(z,x^{\perp}) , target CVs z ′ z^{\prime} , Markov kernels ( M z ) z ∈ ℝ d z \left(M_{z}\right)_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}} , Input: number of steps T T , schedule S ⁡ ( z , z ′ ) = ( z t ) t = 0 T S(z,z^{\prime})=(z_{t})_{t=0}^{T} Initialize x 0 ⟂ = x ⟂ x^{\perp}_{0}=x^{\perp} , for t = 0 ​ … ​ K − 1 t=0\ldots K-1 do Sample x t + 1 ⟂ ∼ M z t ( ⋅ | x t ⟂ ) x^{\perp}_{t+1}\sim M_{z_{t}}(\cdot|x^{\perp}_{t}) , return Final chain of states ( z t , x t ⟂ ) t = 0 T \left(z_{t},x^{\perp}_{t}\right)_{t=0}^{T} This elementary algorithm defines a procedure for proposing a new value of the full state x ′ = ( z ′ , x ⟂ ′ ) = ( z T , x T ⟂ ) x^{\prime}=(z^{\prime},{x^{\perp}}^{\prime})=(z_{T},x_{T}^{\perp}) given a proposed CV update z → z ′ z\rightarrow z^{\prime} . Although, in principle, any Markov kernel M z M_{z} may be used, efficiency of the algorithm described below requires choosing M z M_{z} such that the resulting proposal ( z ′ , x ⟂ ′ ) (z^{\prime},{x^{\perp}}^{\prime}) is likely under the target distribution π \pi . A common and effective choice is a single step of overdamped Langevin dynamics targeting the conditional distribution π ⁡ ( x ⟂ ∣ z ) \pi(x^{\perp}\mid z) at fixed z z : M z ​ ( x t + 1 ⟂ | x t ⟂ ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( x t + 1 ⟂ , x t ⟂ − δ ​ t ​ ∇ x ⟂ U ​ ( z , x t ⟂ ) , 2 ​ δ ​ t ​ I d − d z ) , \displaystyle M_{z}(x^{\perp}_{t+1}|x_{t}^{\perp})=\mathcal{N}\left(x^{\perp}_{t+1};x^{\perp}_{t}-\delta t\nabla_{x^{\perp}}U(z,x^{\perp}_{t}),2\delta tI_{d-d_{z}}\right)\,, (35) where δ ​ t \delta t is a small time-step and U ⁡ ( x ) = − log ⁡ π ⁡ ( x ) U(x)=-\log\pi(x) (up to an additive constant) is the potential energy function associated with the target distribution. Using a Markov kernel Q Q to propose an update of the CV, an accept-reject criterion can be written à la Metropolis-Hastings to design an MCMC with stationary distribution π \pi . For this, the CV-schedule needs to be reversible, meaning that S ⁡ ( z , z ′ ) = ( z t ) t = 0 T S(z,z^{\prime})=(z_{t})_{t=0}^{T} implies that S ⁡ ( z ′ , z ) = ( z T − t ′ ) t ′ = 0 T S(z^{\prime},z)=(z_{T-t^{\prime}})_{t^{\prime}=0}^{T} . The probability density of the generated path and the probability density of following the reverse path with the same protocol are respectively given by Q ⁡ ( z ′ | z ) ​ ∏ t = 0 T − 1 M z t ​ ( x t + 1 ⟂ | x t ⟂ ) , and Q ⁡ ( z | z ′ ) ​ ∏ t ′ = 0 T − 1 M z T − t ′ ​ ( x T − t ′ − 1 ⟂ | x T − t ′ ⟂ ) . \displaystyle Q(z^{\prime}|z)\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}M_{z_{t}}(x^{\perp}_{t+1}|x^{\perp}_{t})\,,\quad\text{and}\quad Q(z|z^{\prime})\prod_{t^{\prime}=0}^{T-1}M_{z_{T-t^{\prime}}}(x^{\perp}_{T-t^{\prime}-1}|x^{\perp}_{T-t^{\prime}})\,. (36) Then a sufficient criterion for ensuring that the overall Markov chain leaves π \pi invariant is to accept the proposed move ( z , x ⟂ ) → ( z ′ , x ⟂ ′ ) (z,x^{\perp})\rightarrow(z^{\prime},{x^{\perp}}^{\prime}) with probability: α = min ⁡ ( 1 , π ⁡ ( z ′ , x ⟂ ′ ) π ⁡ ( z , x ⟂ ) × Q ⁡ ( z | z ′ ) Q ⁡ ( z ′ | z ) × ∏ t ′ = 0 T − 1 M z T − t ′ ​ ( x T − t ′ − 1 ⟂ | x T − t ′ ⟂ ) ∏ t = 0 T − 1 M z t ​ ( x t + 1 ⟂ | x t ⟂ ) ) . \displaystyle\alpha=\min\left(1,\frac{\pi(z^{\prime},{x^{\perp}}^{\prime})}{\pi(z,x^{\perp})}\times\frac{Q(z|z^{\prime})}{Q(z^{\prime}|z)}\times\frac{\prod_{t^{\prime}=0}^{T-1}M_{z_{T-t^{\prime}}}(x^{\perp}_{T-t^{\prime}-1}|x^{\perp}_{T-t^{\prime}})}{\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}M_{z_{t}}(x^{\perp}_{t+1}|x^{\perp}_{t})}\right)\,. (37) This acceptance rule satisfies a property stronger than detailed balance, sometimes referred to as super-detailed balance [ 59 , 130 ] . By using a NF trained to approximate π z \pi_{z} to propose updates in the CV space — that is, by taking Q = ρ θ Q=\rho_{\theta} — one can promote transitions between metastable modes. In turn, this mechanism yields an efficient sampler for complex multimodal distributions. The complete algorithm reads as follows: algorithm 9 Collective-variable guided flow-Monte Carlo (CV-FlowMC) Initialize x ( 0 ) = ( z ( 0 ) , x ⟂ ( 0 ) ) x^{(0)}=(z^{(0)},x^{\perp(0)}) , for k = 1 ​ … ​ K k=1\ldots K do Propose new CVs z ′ ∼ ρ θ ​ ( z ) z^{\prime}\sim\rho_{\theta}(z) , Generate non-eq. path ( z t , x t ⟂ ) t = 0 T \left(z_{t},x^{\perp}_{t}\right)_{t=0}^{T} using algorithm 8 with input ( z ( k − 1 ) , x ⟂ ( k − 1 ) ) (z^{(k-1)},x^{\perp(k-1)}) and z ′ z^{\prime} , Set x ′ = ( z ′ , x T ⟂ ) x^{\prime}=(z^{\prime},x^{\perp}_{T}) , Compute acceptance rate α \alpha using eq. 37 , Set x ( k ) = x ′ x^{(k)}=x^{\prime} with probability α \alpha , else x ( k ) = x ( k − 1 ) x^{(k)}=x^{(k-1)} , return samples { x ( k ) } k = 1 K \{x^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K} Many variants of this algorithm can be envisioned, ranging from technical choices in the definition of the reverse protocol to different selections of the Markov kernels M z M_{z} and associated hyperparameters (e.g., the number of steering steps T T , or the time step δ ​ t \delta t when using overdamped Langevin dynamics). We refer to [ 153 , 154 ] for a detailed analysis of these design choices and their impact on sampler performance. As mentioned above, the method can moreover be extended to arbitrary CV mappings z = ξ ⁡ ( x ) z=\xi(x) by evolving the orthogonal degrees of freedom x ⟂ x^{\perp} at fixed CV values via constrained dynamics, as described in [ 154 ] . Intermediate summary The core idea of combining coarse-graining with flows for sampling is the use of a NF to propose updates in the CV space that traverse low-probability regions and connect metastable modes. Crucially, the flow is trained only in a coarse-grained space ( d z < d d_{z}<d ), whose marginal distribution is typically smoother than the full target distribution π \pi . This substantially alleviates the curse of dimensionality affecting NF-based samplers in the full space, while preserving their ability to generate large, mode-crossing moves. In particular, the admissible dimensionality of the CV space is substantially higher than in traditional CV-based enhanced sampling methods: values on the order of d z ≈ 10 ​ s − 100 ​ s d_{z}\approx 10\text{s}-100\text{s} appear feasible, whereas standard approaches often struggle beyond d z ≈ 3 ​ - ​ 4 d_{z}\approx 3\text{-}4 due to the difficulty of estimating the marginal distribution in higher dimensions with non-parametric methods. Finally, for all the exact samplers leveraging NFs discussed in this section 3 , we have so far assumed that the generative model (either a normalizing flow or an autoregressive model) is trained beforehand to approximate either the full target distribution or its marginal over the CV space. The question of how to train such models efficiently for sampling purposes is, however, a substantial research direction in its own right, to which we now turn.

sections.heading: 4 Training generative models without data
sections.text: In their conventional setting, generative models are trained on large datasets consisting of samples drawn from an unknown target distribution. In scientific computing, the situation is markedly different: the target distribution π \pi is typically known—at least up to a normalization constant—and the central challenge is precisely to generate samples from it. This fundamental distinction calls for a rethinking of the training paradigm. Rather than learning from empirical data, the model must instead exploit direct access to the unnormalized density of the target distribution. In this section, we assume that π ⁡ ( x ) \pi(x) is easy to evaluate up to normalization at any point x x in 𝒳 \mathcal{X} but hard to sample, and we discuss how to leverage this information to train different generative models to approximate π \pi . We organize the discussion according to the main classes of generative models introduced in section 2 . Throughout, we use the notation π = e − U / 𝒵 \pi=e^{-U}/\mathcal{Z} for the target distribution, where U U denotes the potential energy function and 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} the (unknown) normalization constant.

sections.heading: Minimizing the reverse KL divergence
sections.text: Given their tractable likelihood, normalizing flows (NFs) and autoregressive models (ARMs) are typically trained for generative modeling by maximizing the likelihood of the training data. Equivalently, this corresponds to minimizing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the data distribution p data p_{\mathrm{data}} and the model’s distribution ρ θ \rho_{\theta} : D KL ( p data ∥ ρ θ ) = 𝔼 p data [ log p data ​ ( x ) ρ θ ​ ( x ) ] = − ℋ ( p data ) − 𝔼 p data [ log ρ θ ( x ) ] , \displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\mathrm{data}}\|\rho_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}}\left[\log\frac{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}{\rho_{\theta}(x)}\right]=-\mathcal{H}(p_{\mathrm{data}})-\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}}\left[\log\rho_{\theta}(x)\right], (38) where ℋ ⁡ ( p data ) \mathcal{H}(p_{\mathrm{data}}) is the entropy of the data distribution, independent of the model parameters θ \theta . In the context of sampling, however, the “data” distribution is replaced by a target distribution π \pi , and computing expectations with respect to π \pi is typically challenging. There, the reverse KL divergence can serve as a practical training objective instead: D KL ( ρ θ ∥ π ) = 𝔼 ρ θ [ log ρ θ ​ ( x ) π ⁡ ( x ) ] = 𝔼 ρ θ [ log ρ θ ( x ) + U ( x ) ] + log 𝒵 . \displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\rho_{\theta}\|\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{\theta}}\left[\log\frac{\rho_{\theta}(x)}{\pi(x)}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{\theta}}\left[\log\rho_{\theta}(x)+U(x)\right]+\log\mathcal{Z}\,. (39) Expectations with respect to ρ θ \rho_{\theta} are cheap to estimate by drawing independent samples from the NF or ARM, log ⁡ ρ θ \log\rho_{\theta} is available in closed form, and log ⁡ 𝒵 \log\mathcal{Z} is unknown but independent from θ \theta . Minimizing this objective corresponds to variational inference (VI), a well-established technique in Bayesian statistics [ 91 , 19 ] . Variational families for ρ θ \rho_{\theta} must maintain tractable sampling and density evaluation. Traditional choices, such as factorized or Gaussian distributions, are often poorly suited to approximate complex target distributions because they lack flexibility. NFs and ARMs, in contrast, are highly expressive while preserving the required ease of sampling and density evaluation. Using NFs for VI was first proposed by [ 141 ] , who leveraged the reparameterization trick to avoid backpropagating through the sampling process. Writing x ∼ ρ θ x\sim\rho_{\theta} as x = T θ ​ ( z ) x=T_{\theta}(z) with z ∼ ρ 0 z\sim\rho_{0} the base distribution, the effective loss for a batch of N N samples z i ∼ ρ 0 ​ i.i.d. z_{i}\sim\rho_{0}\;\text{i.i.d.} becomes ℓ N ( θ ) = 1 N ∑ i = 1 N [ log ρ 0 ( z i ) − log det | ∇ z T θ ( z i ) | + U ( T θ ( z i ) ) ] . \displaystyle\ell_{N}(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\log\rho_{0}(z_{i})-\log\det\left|\nabla_{z}T_{\theta}(z_{i})\right|+U(T_{\theta}(z_{i}))\right]\,. (40) Following this foundational work, simultaneous applications in statistical physics emerged: [ 5 ] applied NFs to field theories, [ 132 ] to molecular systems – where reverse-KL training is called “training by energy”–, and [ 184 ] to spin systems using ARMs 5 5 5 Here to avoid the issue of having to backpropagate through the sampling process, one compute a Monte Carlo estimator of the training gradients to be plugged into the optimization algorithm rather than applying autodiff directly to the loss estimator (see [ 184 ] ). . However, this seemingly data-free training approach has an important limitation when applied to multimodal target distributions, a phenomenon often referred to as mode collapse.

sections.heading: Mode collapse in VI
sections.text: Mode collapse refers to the tendency of the learned distribution ρ θ \rho_{\theta} to cover only a subset of the modes of the target distribution π \pi . This phenomenon stems from the well-known mode-seeking behavior of the reverse KL divergence: assigning probability mass to regions where π \pi has low density is penalized much more strongly than failing to cover some modes of π \pi altogether [ 91 , 118 ] . Crucially, this behavior is intrinsic to the objective function itself and is therefore not resolved by increasing model expressiveness. As a result, even highly flexible models such as NFs and ARMs can suffer from mode collapse, despite their capacity to represent multimodal distributions, as reported by several authors [ 128 , 20 , 70 ] . This limitation is particularly severe in sampling applications of generative models, since multimodal target distributions are precisely those for which traditional sampling methods struggle the most. A number of heuristic strategies have been proposed to alleviate mode collapse in VI when training exact likelihood models for sampling purposes. For example, [ 132 ] introduced a hybrid training procedure that augments the reverse KL objective with a maximum-likelihood term based on short MCMC trajectories initialized near distinct modes. Alternatively, [ 116 ] proposed estimating the χ 2 \chi^{2} divergence between ρ θ \rho_{\theta} and π \pi using AIS, and minimizing this estimate instead. Another broadly applicable approach consists in combining VI with annealing, which we discuss next.

sections.heading: Annealed VI to mitigate mode collapse
sections.text: A natural strategy to mitigate mode collapse when training NFs is to introduce annealing, in a manner reminiscent of annealed sampling schemes. The key idea is to define a sequence of intermediate distributions ( π k ) k = 0 K \left(\pi_{k}\right)_{k=0}^{K} interpolating between a simple unimodal distribution π 0 \pi_{0} and the target distribution π K = π \pi_{K}=\pi . The model is then trained sequentially: at each stage k k , variational inference (VI) is used to approximate π k \pi_{k} , initializing the parameters of ρ θ k {\rho_{\theta}}_{k} from those obtained at stage k − 1 k-1 . In practice, the intermediate distributions are often defined through tempering of the target distribution, π k ∝ e − β k ​ U \pi_{k}\propto e^{-\beta_{k}U} , with a monotonically increasing sequence of inverse temperatures β 0 < β 1 < … < β K = 1 \beta_{0}<\beta_{1}<\ldots<\beta_{K}=1 or through a geometric interpolation toward a chosen π 0 \pi_{0} , π K ∝ π k / K ​ π 0 ( K − k ) / K \pi_{K}\propto\pi^{k/K}\pi_{0}^{(K-k)/K} . The progressive training strategy along the interpolation path enables the NF to gradually discover and cover distinct modes of the target distribution, thereby reducing the risk of mode collapse. Annealed VI has demonstrated empirical success across a range of applications: the exploration of complex Bayesian posteriors [ 82 , 176 ] , the sampling of Boltzmann distributions in statistical mechanics [ 184 , 73 , 156 ] , and in optimization tasks ranging from locating multiple modes [ 103 ] to identifying global minima [ 78 , 96 , 21 ] . A closely related strategy is employed in the previously discussed (CR)AFT samplers [ 12 , 112 ] , where the flow architecture itself is expanded at each annealing stage by adding new layers, rather than retraining a fixed model. Despite these encouraging results, performance remains highly sensitive to the annealing schedule—most notably the choice of the initial distribution π 0 \pi_{0} and the rate at which the transition is operated toward the target distribution. To date, theoretical guidance on these choices within the VI framework remains limited. Recent work [ 161 , 58 ] , however, has begun to analyze the behavior of (annealed) VI in simplified settings, in particular Gaussian mixture models. In [ 161 ] , the authors identify a critical threshold for the separation between modes—dependent on their relative weights but independent of the ambient dimension—that determines whether mode collapse occurs. This behavior is also observed empirically when training NFs on Gaussian mixtures. Building on this analysis, [ 58 ] derive a closed-form expression for the probability of mode collapse in the bimodal Gaussian mixture case, enabling a more detailed study of the impact of the annealing schedule. Their results confirm the mitigating role of annealing and provide concrete guidance for its practical implementation: starting from a sufficiently high temperature is not, by itself, sufficient—one must also ensure that the annealing schedule is slow enough. These theoretical predictions are again supported by experiments with NFs trained on Gaussian mixtures. These works constitute an important first step toward a more rigorous understanding of (annealed) VI with expressive generative models, such as ARMs and NFs, and offer valuable insight for its use in challenging sampling applications.

sections.heading: 4.1.2 Adaptive strategies
sections.text: While training exact likelihood models via the reverse KL divergence requires explicit safeguards against mode collapse—such as annealing—an alternative line of work has focused on retaining the standard and notably stable maximum-likelihood training paradigm, equivalent to eq. 38 . Because direct samples from the target distribution π \pi are not available, these approaches rely on adaptive strategies in which data collection and model training are interleaved. This idea was first introduced by [ 136 ] in the context of triangular transport maps, independently extended to general variational families by [ 123 ] , and later rediscovered for modern NFs in [ 60 , 61 ] . We summarize the latter approach below (which is straightforwardly applicable to ARMs as well). The adaptive training procedure runs an MCMC chain targeting π \pi , which alternates between two types of Markov update kernels: (i) A local MCMC kernel (e.g., Langevin dynamics or Hamiltonian Monte Carlo) that leaves π \pi invariant and explores the target distribution, denoted M π M_{\pi} below; (ii) A global NF-based kernel that also leaves π \pi invariant – such as the flow-independent Metropolis-Hastings kernel described in algorithm 2 –and enables long-range, mode-crossing updates, denoted M ρ θ M_{\rho_{\theta}} below. The NF is periodically retrained by maximum likelihood on the samples collected so far, leading to the following overall scheme: algorithm 10 Adaptive flow Monte Carlo (A-flowMC) Input: Initial NF parameters θ \theta , learning rate η \eta , frequency of global jumps K g K_{g} , frequency of retraining K t K_{t} Initialize x ( 0 , m ) x^{(0,m)} for m = 1 ​ … ​ M m=1\ldots M in basins of attraction of the distinct modes of π \pi for k = 1 ​ … ​ K k=1\ldots K do if k mod K g = 0 k\mod K_{g}=0 then Global NF-based move x ( k , m ) ∼ M ρ θ ( ⋅ | x ( k − 1 , m ) ) x^{(k,m)}\sim M_{\rho_{\theta}}(\cdot|x^{(k-1,m)}) else Local MCMC move x ( k , m ) ∼ M π ( ⋅ | x ( k − 1 , m ) ) x^{(k,m)}\sim M_{\pi}(\cdot|x^{(k-1,m)}) if k mod K t = 0 k\mod K_{t}=0 then θ ← θ + η M ​ k ​ ∑ m = 1 M ∑ ℓ = 1 k ∇ log ⁡ ρ θ ​ ( x ( ℓ , m ) ) \displaystyle\theta\leftarrow\theta+\frac{\eta}{Mk}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\nabla\log\rho_{\theta}(x^{(\ell,m)}) return trained flow ρ θ \rho_{\theta} , samples ( x ( k , m ) ) m , k = 1 M , K \left(x^{(k,m)}\right)_{m,k=1}^{M,K} Variants of this basic scheme include discarding the oldest samples to limit memory usage and improve equilibration, subsampling mini-batches from previously collected samples, performing multiple gradient steps at each retraining stage, and using more advanced optimizers such as Adam instead of simple stochastic gradient descent (SGD). The key feature of this approach is that it simultaneously achieves two objectives: it produces unbiased samples from the target distribution π \pi , and it trains a NF (or an ARM) that can subsequently be used within an efficient standalone sampler from section 3 . From a theoretical standpoint, however, proving convergence of such adaptive MCMC schemes—where the transition kernel evolves over time based on the history of the chain and thus violates the Markov property—is non-trivial [ 23 ] . In particular, convergence of the Markov chain to the target measure π \pi typically requires the adaptation to vanish asymptotically. In practice, this issue can be sidestepped by stopping the training once the NF is deemed sufficiently accurate, and then continuing the simulation with a fixed kernel to generate exact samples from π \pi . The benefit of alternating between local and global moves is that the two components reinforce each other. Local MCMC updates explore individual modes in detail, providing training data that allow the NF to capture local structure, while the NF enables global proposals that help the chain escape metastable states. Together, these mechanisms facilitate accurate estimation of the relative weights of the different modes. Rigorous analyses demonstrating the advantages of combining local and global sampling have been established for NFs in [ 147 ] and for ARMs in [ 44 , 21 ] . Provided that the MCMC chains can be initialized in all modes of interest of the target distribution, the maximum-likelihood objective naturally prevents mode collapse, since all modes present in the training data must be represented by the generative model. A notable exception arises for modes that are significantly rarer than others: in this case, some training batches may contain no samples from these rare modes, causing the NF to accidentally forget them. This issue can be mitigated by enforcing that training batches include samples from all relevant modes, or by using a mixture of models in which each component is trained on a specific mode and the mixture weights are lower bounded [ 60 , 73 , 119 ] . Aside from these rare-mode scenario—which requires special care—the main limitation of adaptive strategies based on maximum-likelihood training remains the need to initialize chains in all relevant modes. As for mode collapse, this limitation can be alleviated by resorting to annealing, as discussed next.

sections.heading: 4.1.3 Sequential tempering
sections.text: The idea of adaptive maximum-likelihood training can be easily combined with annealing in order to relax the assumption that all relevant modes of the target distribution are known in advance. This sequential tempering is therefore built upon an annealing schedule ( π k ) k = 0 K \left(\pi_{k}\right)_{k=0}^{K} defined, as before, with π 0 \pi_{0} a simple, typically unimodal distribution and π K = π \pi_{K}=\pi the target distribution and follows an iterative procedure. The algorithm is initialized by sampling from π 0 \pi_{0} using a suitable MCMC method, a task that is assumed to be straightforward. An exact likelihood model is then trained by maximum likelihood on the resulting samples from π 0 \pi_{0} . Once trained, the generative model is used to facilitate sampling from the slightly more challenging distribution π 1 \pi_{1} , for instance via flow/ARM-independent Metropolis-Hastings ( algorithm 2 ). The samples collected at this stage are used in turn to retrain the generative model by maximum likelihood, initializing the optimization from the parameters learned at the previous level. This procedure is repeated along the annealing path until the target distribution π K \pi_{K} is reached, leading to the following overall scheme: algorithm 11 Sequential tempering Input: Initial NF parameters θ \theta , learning rate η \eta x ( 0 , m ) ∼ π 0 x^{(0,m)}\sim\pi_{0} using MCMC for m = 1 ​ … ​ M m=1\ldots M for k = 0 ​ … ​ K − 1 k=0\ldots K-1 do repeat θ ← θ + η M ​ ∑ m = 1 M ∇ θ ​ log ​ ρ θ ​ ( x ( k , m ) ) \displaystyle\theta\leftarrow\theta+\frac{\eta}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\nabla_{\theta}\log\rho_{\theta}(x^{(k,m)}) until convergence x ( k + 1 , m ) ∼ x^{(k+1,m)}\sim flow/ARM-IMH targeting π k + 1 \pi_{k+1} using current ρ θ \rho_{\theta} for m = 1 ​ … ​ M m=1\ldots M return trained flow ρ θ \rho_{\theta} , samples ( x ( K , m ) ) m = 1 M \left(x^{(K,m)}\right)_{m=1}^{M} Training the flow to convergence at each annealing stage robustly prevents mode collapse, provided that the annealing schedule is sufficiently fine. This conservative strategy was termed “adiabatic retraining” by [ 73 ] . In practice, however, it may be computationally more efficient to perform only a limited number of training steps at each stage, in the same spirit as adaptive training without annealing ( algorithm 10 ). Note that, in the same spirit, [ 25 ] proposed an annealed adaptive training for flow matchings ( section 2.4 ), replacing the maximum-likelihood objective with the likelihood-free flow-matching loss eq. 22 , and substituting the independent Metropolis-Hastings sampler with a sampler related to NeutraMCMC, which however requires the costly evaluation of the flow Jacobian determinant. This sequential tempering strategy has been primarily explored in the context of sampling disordered spin systems using autoregressive models, beginning with the work of [ 113 ] and subsequently adopted in [ 35 , 44 , 21 ] . Such settings are particularly well suited to sequential tempering, as the number and location of modes are typically unknown. Nevertheless, the approach may still fail to produce exact samples when the target distribution is too complex to be faithfully represented by the chosen model class. This limitation was illustrated in [ 35 ] , where autoregressive models were found to be inadequate for sampling solutions of a graph-coloring constraint satisfaction problem. Going further, [ 35 ] analyze the mechanisms underlying these failures by comparing different training objectives, namely VI and maximum-likelihood training with tempering. VI tends to produce approximations ρ θ \rho_{\theta} that underestimate the entropy of π \pi , in line with the mode collapse phenomenon, while still generating configurations with appropriate energies. In contrast, maximum-likelihood training accurately captures the entropy but often yields configurations with energies higher than those of the true equilibrium distribution. While this study focused on autoregressive models, similar phenomena are likely to arise when training normalizing flows under either objective. To move beyond these limitations, one can consider alternative classes of generative models amenable to different training objectives, as detailed in the next sections.

sections.heading: 4.2 Continuous annealed flows
sections.text: Continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) based on ODEs are typically more expressive than their discrete counterparts. However, evaluating their likelihood (see eq. 10 ) is computationally demanding and inevitably subject to discretization error. Consequently, the training methods described in the previous sections for "discrete-time" normalizing flows are not well suited to the continuous setting. Instead, one can exploit the intrinsic continuity of CNFs and train them for sampling by matching the trajectories of the flow to a prescribed annealing path of distributions. Here we consider a path ( π t ) t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \left(\pi_{t}\right)_{t\in[0,1]} indexed by a continuous time t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] , with π 0 \pi_{0} a simple distribution and π 1 = π \pi_{1}=\pi the target. This approach was first developed for deterministic continuous flows (as CNFs presented in section 2.2.2 ). It was subsequently extended to a stochastic variant, which we discuss afterward. A summary of the different training settings for continuous flows is provided in table 1 .

sections.heading: Langevin-driven stochastic flows
Learning the annealing path jointly with the dynamics
sections.text: Finally, we note that within this framework it has also been proposed to learn the annealing path ( π t ) t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] (\pi_{t})_{t\in[0,1]} itself, in addition to the velocity field and the free energy [ 111 , 9 ] . This additional layer of learning is motivated by the observation that, as for any annealing based sampling or training approach, the choice of path can have a substantial impact on sampling performance. In particular, phase transitions along the path—namely abrupt changes in the localization or relative weights of the modes—are expected to severely hinder sampling efficiency. In [ 111 ] , the energy U t U_{t} is treated as a trainable function of the form U θ , t = t ​ U 1 + ( 1 − t ) ​ U 0 + t ⁡ ( 1 − t ) ​ U ^ θ , t \displaystyle{U_{\theta,t}=tU_{1}+(1-t)U_{0}+t(1-t)\hat{U}_{\theta,t}} (51) where U ^ θ , t \hat{U}_{\theta,t} is parameterized by a neural network. The authors minimize the same PINN loss eq. 46 jointly over v θ v_{\theta} , F θ F_{\theta} , and U θ U_{\theta} . The resulting objective is likely to admit many solutions, and it remains unclear how to systematically favor those leading to favorable sampling properties. Nevertheless, this approach constitutes a first step toward learning annealing paths automatically, and encouraging numerical results are reported in simple settings where traditional annealing schemes of geometrical averaging or temperature scheduling struggle. In contrast, the more recent work [ 9 ] advocate for learning the energy function associated with the marginal distribution of a stochastic interpolant (see eq. 18 ) deriving yet again another PINN loss. The appeal of this choice is not accidental: stochastic interpolant bridges are typically smooth and regular, thereby avoiding the sharp transitions and mode switching that plague many traditional annealing paths. This regularity is also characteristic of diffusion models and partly underlies the considerable attention they have received for sampling applications, as discussed in the next section. Namely, we now turn to examine how diffusion models can be trained for sampling purposes.

sections.heading: 4.3 Diffusion models
sections.text: Due to the stochastic nature of the generative process, likelihood evaluation for diffusion models is even less tractable than for continuous normalizing flows (CNFs), for which the variational and adaptive training methods presented in section 2.2.2 are already of limited practical suitability. Moreover, diffusion models inherently define their own bridging path between a simple reference distribution and the target, and therefore cannot be trained to follow a prescribed annealing path as CNFs. For these reasons, diffusion models have prompted the development of a distinct family of training objectives tailored to sampling. The reader interested in disordered statistical physics system and high-dimensional statistics should refer to [ 4 , 121 , 120 , 65 ] . In these special instances, the score can be computed using message passing algorithms. We do not discuss these approaches here and focus instead on general purpose strategies. We begin by clarifying the challenges associated with likelihood estimation in diffusion models ( section 4.3.1 ) before turning to alternative training approaches that circumvent explicit likelihood computation ( sections 4.3.2 and 4.3.3 ). The different approaches presented are summarized in table 1 .

Since the score of a distribution is sufficient to sample from it using Langevin dynamics, [ 69 ] proposes to run a Langevin-within-Langevin dynamics to initialize X t 0 ∼ π T − t 0 X_{t_{0}}\sim\pi_{T-t_{0}} , before proceeding with the same denoising procedure as in [ 83 ] . The resulting algorithm named stochastic localization through iterative posterior sampling (SLIPS) is summarized in algorithm 14 . The original formulation of SLIPS uses the stochastic localization process as the outer denoising dynamics. This process can be viewed as a variant of the denoising dynamics that starts from a Dirac distribution at t = 0 t=0 rather than from a Gaussian. Its name originates from the stochastic localization framework introduced in [ 53 , 54 , 55 , 31 ] , where it was developed as a tool to establish results in geometric measure theory. However, the same idea can also be applied to the standard denoising dynamics used in diffusion models, leading to the algorithm described in algorithm 14 . algorithm 14 Stochastic localization through iterative posterior sampling (SLIPS) Input: Initialization time t 0 t_{0} , number of denoising steps K K , time horizon T T , time scheduling { t k } k = 1 K \{t_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} with t K = T t_{K}=T , number of Langevin steps L L , number of Langevin chains N N , Langevin step size η \eta Initialize X t 0 X_{t_{0}} randomly for ℓ = 1 ​ … ​ L \ell=1\ldots L do Estimate the score s ^ ​ ( t 0 , X t 0 ) \hat{s}(t_{0},X_{t_{0}}) by running algorithm 12 X t 0 ← X t 0 + η ⁡ ( X t 0 + 2 ​ s ^ ​ ( t 0 , X t 0 ) ) + 2 ​ η ​ ξ ℓ X_{t_{0}}\leftarrow X_{t_{0}}+\eta ig(X_{t_{0}}+2\hat{s}(t_{0},X_{t_{0}}) ig)+\sqrt{2\eta}\,\xi_{\ell} , with ξ ℓ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \xi_{\ell}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) for k = 1 ​ … ​ K k=1\ldots K do Δ ​ t k = t k − t k − 1 \Delta t_{k}=t_{k}-t_{k-1} Estimate the score s ^ ​ ( t k , X k − 1 ) \hat{s}(t_{k},X_{k-1}) by running algorithm 12 Update X k = X k − 1 + ( X k − 1 + 2 ​ s ^ ​ ( t k , X k − 1 ) ) ​ Δ ​ t k + 2 ​ Δ ​ t k ​ ξ k X_{k}=X_{k-1}+ ig(X_{k-1}+2\hat{s}(t_{k},X_{k-1}) ig)\Delta t_{k}+\sqrt{2\Delta t_{k}}\,\xi_{k} , with ξ k ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \xi_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) return X K X_{K} Starting at t 0 > 0 t_{0}>0 allows the algorithm to bypass the multimodality of q 0 | T − t ( ⋅ | x ) q_{0|T-t}(\cdot|x) at earlier times t < t 0 t<t_{0} , but it also introduces an additional source of error associated with the initialization of the denoising process. The quality of this initialization now depends on the ability of Langevin dynamics to sample from π T − t 0 \pi_{T-t_{0}} . In contrast to the conditional distribution q 0 | T − t ( ⋅ | x ) q_{0|T-t}(\cdot|x) , the distribution π T − t 0 \pi_{T-t_{0}} is unimodal for t 0 t_{0} small enough (since π T ≈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \pi_{T}\approx\mathcal{N}(0,I) , see again illustration of fig. 5 ). Hence, the approach of [ 69 ] accommodates multimodal target distributions π \pi at the cost of identifying a suitable starting time t 0 t_{0} at which both π T − t 0 \pi_{T-t_{0}} and q 0 | T − t 0 ( ⋅ | x ) q_{0|T-t_{0}}(\cdot|x) are unimodal, or more conservatively log-concave. This requirement is referred to as the duality of concavity . Such a regime is not guaranteed to exist for all target distributions π \pi . [ 69 ] identifies a class of distributions for which the duality of log-concavity condition can be satisfied and demonstrated in numerical experiments accurate sampling of multimodal distributions beyond this class. However, determining the appropriate starting time t 0 t_{0} in general remains an open question. As an alternative to the standard denoising score matching loss used to train diffusion models from data, [ 83 , 69 ] discussed above propose Monte Carlo estimators of the score. These approaches eliminate the need to train a neural network altogether by performing score estimation on the fly during the denoising sampling process, thereby yielding non-parametric methods. While this strategy avoids issues related to model misspecification, it precludes any form of amortization of the score estimation. A natural extension in this direction, discussed in the following paragraphs, is to regress a parametric score model onto the Monte Carlo estimates, enabling faster resampling once training is completed.

sections.heading: Adaptive regression of a Monte Carlo estimator of the score
sections.text: Let s ^ ​ ( x , τ ) \hat{s}(x,\tau) be a Monte Carlo estimator of the score ∇ log ⁡ π τ ​ ( x ) \nabla\log\pi_{\tau}(x) . In order to amortize the score estimation, one can train a parametric model s θ ​ ( x , τ ) s_{\theta}(x,\tau) by regressing it onto s ^ ​ ( x , τ ) \hat{s}(x,\tau) . Since it is unrealistic to expect s ^ ​ ( x , τ ) \hat{s}(x,\tau) to be accurate everywhere in the state space, a key question is how to select the points at which the regression loss should be evaluated. Ideally, the learned score should be accurate in regions of high probability under π τ \pi_{\tau} that are likely to be visited during the denoising process. In the absence of training data, however, achieving such localization is extremely challenging In a philosophy closely related to the adaptive training strategies for normalizing flows described in section 4.1.2 , the approach proposed by [ 3 ] leverages the availability of a small number of low-quality target samples, which in particular provide information about the location of the different modes. These initial samples are used to initialize a buffer of datapoints. Points from this buffer are used as initial conditions for noising trajectories to generate an initial set of points on which the regression loss is evaluated. The learned score model is subsequently used to generate new denoised samples, which are added to the buffer, and the procedure is then repeated. This iterative scheme allows the score model to progressively improve its accuracy in regions of high probability under π t \pi_{t} that are most relevant for sampling from π \pi . Using a mean squared regression loss, and a simple Euler-Maruyama discretization of the noising process, the resulting algorithm can be sketched as follows: algorithm 15 Iterated score regression In practice, however, importance sampling is not expected to scale well to high-dimensional settings. Nevertheless, the idea of amortizing score estimations through a regression model evaluated on an adaptive buffer of samples is appealing. Overall, the remaining open question in this line of research estimating the score by Monte Carlo concerns the choice of the sampler for the estimator, as both Langevin dynamics and importance sampling suffer from intrinsic limitations, as discussed above.

sections.text:
Another line of work, which bypasses both the need to estimate likelihoods and the need for training samples when learning diffusion models, exploits the connection between diffusion models and stochastic optimal control problems [ 170 , 189 , 17 , 173 , 142 , 186 , 131 , 75 ] . This connection can also be interpreted through the lens of variational inference. Without aiming for full mathematical rigor, we provide below a high-level sketch of this relationship. The resulting training objective eq. 64 directly reads as a stochastic optimal control problem, with u θ u_{	heta} playing the role of the control. The control is learned so as to minimize a cost functional balancing a running cost ∫ 0 T ‖ u θ ​ ( X t , T − t ) ‖ 2 ​ 𝑑 t \int_{0}^{T}\|u_{	heta}(X_{t},T-t)\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t , which penalizes deviations from the reference process, and a terminal cost log ⁡ ρ ref ​ ( X T ) e − U ⁡ ( X T ) \log rac{ho_{	ext{ref}}(X_{T})}{e^{-U(X_{T})}} , which encourages the terminal state X T X_{T} to follow the target distribution π \pi . This objective can be optimized by sampling trajectories from the variational path measure ℙ θ \mathbb{P}_{	heta} and evaluating the cost functional along these trajectories. The tractability of the scores of the reference process ensures that ℙ θ \mathbb{P}_{	heta} can be sampled efficiently, while the terminal cost only requires evaluating the unnormalized density of the target distribution π \pi . This formulation provides a principled way to train diffusion models for sampling without access to a training dataset or to the likelihood of the model. However, this training objective is computationally expensive, as it requires re-sampling, and backpropagating through, trajectories from the variational path measure ℙ θ \mathbb{P}_{	heta} at each training iteration to evaluate the gradients of the cost functional. To alleviate this cost, [ 142 ] proposes an alternative objective, termed the log-variance loss. In place of the KL–that is, the expectation under the variational measure of the logarithm of the Radon-Nikodym derivative between the variational and target path measures–, the log-variance loss is the variance of this same log-derivative with respect to an arbitrary path measure ℙ ^ \mathbb{\hat{P}} : D LV ( ℙ θ ∥ ℙ π ) \displaystyle D_{\mathrm{LV}}(\mathbb{P}_{	heta}\|\mathbb{P}_{\pi}) = 𝕍 ℙ ^ ​ [ log ⁡ d ​ ℙ θ d ​ ℙ π ] . \displaystyle=\mathbb{V}_{\mathbb{\hat{P}}}\left[\log rac{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{	heta}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{\pi}}ight]. (65) This quantity can also be re-expressed into a tractable form using the reference process (see appendix C ). The possibility to use an arbitrary path measure ℙ ^ \mathbb{\hat{P}} to evaluate the variance provides additional flexibility and circumvents the need to backpropagate trough trajectories. In practice, a common choice remains ℙ ^ = StopGrad ⁡ ( ℙ θ ) \mathbb{\hat{P}}=\mathrm{StopGrad}(\mathbb{P}_{	heta}) 8 8 8 The dependence in the trainable parameters of the argument of StopGrad is ignored during learning. as in the original KL formulation, albeit potentially re-using a buffer of trajectories generated at previous values of θ 	heta . The log-variance loss is shown to exhibit lower variance and, to some extent, to be less prone to mode collapse than the traditional KL objective. Among other attempts to reduce computational cost, [ 186 ] uses partial trajectories and [ 75 ] leverages the adjoint method to compute gradients of the KL divergence with respect to θ 	heta , showing that under some conditions the adjoint-base objective can be heuristically simplified to avoid systematic resampling of trajectories at each training iteration. Beyond these computational considerations, two additional aspects of the variational approach warrant careful examination: the parametrization of the control and the choice of the reference distribution ρ ref ho_{	ext{ref}} . Concerning the control, [ 76 ] show that a so-called Langevin preconditioning , first introduced by [ 189 ] , is necessary for the resulting generative process to properly cover the target distribution. This preconditioning consists in informing the score of the variational path measure ℙ θ \mathbb{P}_{	heta} with the score of the target distribution π \pi following: s θ ( x , t ) = s θ 1 , θ 2 ( x , t ) = NN θ 1 ( x , t ) + NN θ 2 ( t ) ∇ log π ( x ) , \displaystyle s_{	heta}(x,t)=s_{	heta_{1},	heta_{2}}(x,t)=	ext{NN}_{	heta_{1}}(x,t)+	ext{NN}_{	heta_{2}}(t)
abla\log\pi(x), (66) with NN θ 1 : ℝ d × [ 0 , 1 ] → ℝ d 	ext{NN}_{	heta_{1}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}	imes[0,1]	o\mathbb{R}^{d} and NN θ 2 : [ 0 , 1 ] → ℝ 	ext{NN}_{	heta_{2}}:[0,1]	o\mathbb{R} neural networks initialized such that NN θ 1 ≈ 0 d 	ext{NN}_{	heta_{1}}\approx 0_{d} and NN θ 2 ≈ 1 	ext{NN}_{	heta_{2}}\approx 1 at initialization. This parametrization ensures that, in the early stages of training, the denoising process closely resembles a Langevin dynamics targeting the distribution π \pi , and therefore will progressively locate high-probability regions of the target. Concerning the path measure, in principle, any ℙ ref \mathbb{P}_{	ext{ref}} can be used within the variational framework, provided that the scores of the noised marginals ρ ref , τ ho_{	ext{ref},	au} remain tractable. In practice, however, the choice of ρ ref ho_{	ext{ref}} has a significant impact on training outcomes, particularly when targeting multimodal distributions, as evidenced by [ 131 ] . In that work, the prescriptions of [ 189 ] and [ 173 ] to use a Gaussian reference distribution are shown to recover the correct mode weights of a bimodal target distribution only when the reference corresponds to the best Gaussian approximation of the target, even when using the more favorable log-variance training objective. This observation motivates an alternative strategy. Acknowledging the need to adapt the reference distribution to the target in order to address the challenges posed by multimodality, [ 131 ] propose a pretraining strategy that learns the reference distribution ρ ref ho_{	ext{ref}} itself. As in adaptive methods for NFs and in the iterated score regression approach discussed earlier, this learning procedure leverages a small number of low-quality samples from the target distribution π \pi , which in particular provide information about the location of the modes. These initial samples can be used either to fit a Gaussian mixture model as ρ ref ho_{	ext{ref}} or to train a time-dependent energy-based model ρ ref , τ ho_{	ext{ref},	au} , for both of which the scores of the noised marginals are tractable. The resulting learned reference distribution is then employed to define the variational path measure ℙ θ \mathbb{P}_{	heta} and to train the control u θ u_{	heta} , as described above. This approach is shown to significantly improve the performance of the resulting sampler on multimodal targets. Intermediate summary We have now reviewed the main approaches proposed to train autoregressive models, normalizing flows—both in their discrete and continuous formulations—as well as diffusion models, in the sampling setting, where no training data from the target distribution are available a priori. For exact likelihood generative models, autoregressive models and discrete-time normalizing flows, the conceptual picture is essentially complete: as discussed in section 3 , once the model has been trained to approximate the target distribution, it can be embedded within sampling schemes offering rigorous convergence guarantees. For continuous-time models—namely continuous NFs and diffusion models—more remains to be said. The exact sampling strategies presented in section 3 rely critically on the ability to evaluate the model likelihood, a property that is readily available for discrete-time NFs but generally challenging in continuous time. This fundamental obstacle prevents a direct transposition of those constructions. We now turn to the first proposals in the literature that aim to overcome this difficulty and to construct exact samplers leveraging the generative capabilities of continuous-time models.
